items.title: AI coding got faster. Why didn’t engineering?
items.summary: AI is great at making individuals faster, but the surrounding systems are then slowing everything right back down. This result — or, rather, lack thereof — is amplified by company size and pull request size. To the point that, while AI investment has increased 28 times for most companies, and especially those with more than 99 engineers, velocity measures are stagnant and even down. Such is the finding of the recently released State of AI Impact in Engineering from DX, which measures engineering organizations across speed, effectiveness, quality, and impact . Justin Reock , deputy CTO of DX, tells The New Stack , “It is concerning because, when the cost has gone up 28x — which, literally, the only exponential metric is cost — and velocity is not exponential, we’re not shipping exponentially more.” While AI spend continues to skyrocket, the innovation ratio — the allocation of engineering effort spent on new feature work versus maintenance, toil, and operational overhead — remains flat. This means AI is not freeing up engineers’ time to spend on interesting business solutions, according to the report. How is the industry spending so much more money on agentic and AI developer tools, while also doing layoffs, to no avail? Read on as we dive into these disturbing metrics. Is developer experience trending down? “It is possible that we’re still in this inflection point where a lot of this saved time is still just being spent on tech debt, backlog stuff that may not necessarily be tagged as a new feature,” Reock says, still hopeful that the gap between the AI cost and benefit is just growing pains. “But then, on the developer experience side of things, the specific tension in the report between code maintainability and change confidence is also concerning to me.” These two drivers make up the Developer Experience Index (DXI) benchmark: Code maintainability – I feel comfortable making changes to the code. I can understand the code in front of me. Change confidence – I feel confident that when I release code into production, I will not break things. Traditionally, code maintainability and change confidence have positively correlated, Reock explains, because the first makes engineers more comfortable releasing the second to production. “AI is making it easier to understand what’s in front of you, and even to make changes to it. But change confidence is now in the negatives,” he says. “We’re more afraid to release the code. So we can understand the code, maintain the code, look at the code, and make changes to it more easily. But we trust less what we’re releasing.” Which is costing even more. For every point of improvement in DXI, he explains, you return ten hours a year to each engineer. This is the first time that DX has witnessed a drop in this measurement, by two points industrywide. Is AI the square peg to enterprises’ round hole? Smaller organizations spend more on AI and get more out of it, DX finds, while legacy software organizations are struggling to see any return on investment. This is what he calls the renovation problem , where some of these structures aren’t fit for purpose anymore. “You can’t retrofit this. Can you improve what you don’t measure? According to research from LeadDev’s AI Impact Report 2026 , due to publish later this August, only 31% of teams interviewed are measuring AI’s impact at all. LeadDev defined these measurements as: Real productivity gains Security risk Retention of core engineering skills Agentic AI governance Team restructuring Junior hiring and training Among organizations that have actually started adopting AI-powered developer tools, the LeadDev report finds 70% now describe themselves as having adopted “widely or completely,” with only 26% reporting that AI has boosted engineering productivity by more than 25%. That 26%, Michael Hill , managing editor at LeadDev and report author, clarifies, includes respondents going on instinct, not just confirmed data. “The productivity optimism — 26% seeing big gains — and the measurement gap — only 31% actually tracking it — are two separate findings from two different questions,” Hill tells The New Stack , which means that “most of the people reporting gains aren’t the same people who can prove it.” As we know, engineering is a science, so you can’t improve what you don’t measure. But even for those measuring it, the results are worrying. Reock points to the DXI score going down for the first time last quarter: “We should really be paying attention to that because our customer base trends up, right? The data is heavily biased because they [DX customers] are investing in developer experience, like actively. They bought a product, and so that number tends to trend upward for our cohort of customers. So to see this actually go down is very concerning.” The post AI coding got faster. items.title: I was a New York psychologist who thought I understood families. Then I moved to Wichita.
items.summary: I (not pictured) learned a lot from my time living in Wichita, Kansas. LightFieldStudios/Getty Images/iStockphoto I finished my postdoctoral training in New York City, where I worked with families and kids. After moving to Wichita, I saw just how thriving families can look so different in different places. A healthy dynamic doesn't look the same for every family, and I've taken this lesson into my work. The drive-thru line at Chick-fil-A stretched around the block, packed with oversized SUVs at 10 a.m. on a Tuesday. Engines idled. No one honked. No one seemed in a hurry. It was one of my first glimpses of life in Wichita, and it felt like a different world. I had just finished my postdoctoral training in New York City, where I had worked with children and families in a wide range of settings. I was confident I understood family systems. I had the degrees, the supervised clinical hours, and the professional language to explain how families function under pressure . Then I had my first son, and my husband's job brought us to Wichita. Here, I found a dramatically different rhythm Living in Wichita showed me new perspectives. gnagel/iStock Geography dictates many things, from food to recreational activities. Despite a plethora of farms, fresh produce felt scarce in many areas. Flat vistas, no ocean in sight, and real tornado threats. Yes, Dorothy, I was really in Kansas. Community looked different in this Midwestern city, too. Sunday mornings were quiet: no lawn mowers, no delivery trucks — not because nothing was "happening," but because people were at church, had personal commitments, and reason to pause in a way I had never seen on the East Coast. In New York City, Sunday mornings meant brunch reservations and open inboxes ahead of the workweek. What struck me most was the way people spoke, and the naturally unrushed pace of speech. There was no impulse to fill the silence. No one really said, "We should get lunch sometime," with no intention of doing it. If someone said they would call you, they called you. If they said they would show up, they showed up. On the East and West Coasts, where I had lived as a child, I had grown fluent in a kind of conversational currency where words were placeholders for intentions that may or may not exist. In Wichita, people meant what they said and said what they meant. I remember thinking, quietly and repeatedly, that this was a beautiful thing. Professionally, Wichita taught me a lot As a clinician trained to assess family systems, I did not experience my new life as merely observation. I experienced it as data. I had spent years learning to recognize healthy functioning against a fairly narrow, unspoken standard, one shaped almost entirely by the fast, achievement-oriented environment I trained in. Watching an entirely different rhythm operate successfully, with its own coherence, its own values, its own quiet integrity, was not something my training had prepared me to see up close. The lesson was not that one rhythm is correct and the other is not. The lesson was that families do not follow a single template for pace, values, or connection. A family can be thriving while looking almost nothing like the families I had been trained to recognize as thriving. It is easy, especially coming out of a field trained heavily in one regional context, to mistake familiarity for health. A fast-paced, achievement-oriented family is not inherently dysfunctional. Neither is a slower, more relationship-centered one, built around Costco runs and Sunday mornings and saying exactly what you mean. What matters clinically is whether a family's own rhythm is actually working for them, not whether it resembles the one I happened to experience myself growing up and in my training. These lessons stayed with me long after I left Kansas Knowing where a family is from can teach you a lot. bernardbodo/Getty Images Today, I'm based in Pennsylvania, though my work takes me into homes across the country. Every family brings its own history, community, geography, values, and way of moving through the world. Those influences don't exist outside the family system. They are woven into it. Now, whenever I conduct an intake for a clinical evaluation or a school-admissions strategy session, one of the first questions I ask parents is, "Where are you from?" I want to know not only where they live now, but also about the roots that shaped them long before their child was born. My training taught me how to recognize patterns. Wichita taught me to ask where those patterns came from before deciding whether they needed to change. Every place we live leaves its imprint on a family. The communities we call or have called home shape our expectations, beliefs, and even the way we communicate with each other. Understanding a family means understanding and accepting those roots, not as a point of comparison, but as a foundation to a healthy dynamic. Read the original article on Business Insider

In Wichita, people meant what they said and said what they meant. I remember thinking, quietly and repeatedly, that this was a beautiful thing.

As a clinician trained to assess family systems, I did not experience my new life as merely observation. I experienced it as data.

items.title: Taiwan's war drills showcased a new strike drone class that Ukraine used to smash Russia this year
items.summary: A fixed-wing "mid-size" drone was displayed at the Han Kuang exercises this year. Ann Wang/REUTERS Taiwan showcased two midsize strike drones above its southwest coast on Saturday. Their designs and descriptions draw easy comparisons to Ukraine's mid-range drones. Such drones likely give Taiwan the ability to cheaply hit a Chinese invasion force over the horizon. ZUOYING, TAIWAN — Taiwan's navy deployed two medium-class strike drones on Saturday for the island's biggest annual military exercise, and their designs resemble those of the loitering munitions giving Ukraine fresh wins against Russia this year. The pair of fixed-wing, propeller-driven drones appeared during a littoral combat drill simulating an attack on Zuoying, Taiwan's southwest coast. It was the first time these drones were shown at the Han Kuang exercise , Taiwan's annual rehearsals against a Chinese invasion. As the drones loitered for about 30 minutes above the beach, Taiwanese military officials described them to reporters as "medium-size suicide drones," adding they were locally built. The island's National Chung-Shan Institute of Science and Technology designs and manufactures the vast majority of Taiwan's homegrown weapons. "The drone used was provided by the Armament Bureau to the navy for testing purpose," a spokesperson for Taiwan's navy told Business Insider. They declined to comment on the drone's specifications or whether its design was influenced in any way by the recent wars in Ukraine or the Middle East. The one-way drones were not shown attempting to launch an attack, and it's unclear whether they represent Taiwan's final designs for the aircraft. Ukraine has been using similar fixed-wing drones to attack Russian forces roughly 30 to 300 km behind the front lines this year, mainly disrupting supply routes that the Kremlin has relied on to funnel resources to the war. Zuoying, where Taiwan hosts its largest naval base, is about 295 km, or 183 miles, from mainland China. "The desire to employ more medium-range drones fits into things that Taiwan has learned from Ukraine, " said Bryce Barros, a visiting fellow at the Institute for National Defense and Security Research, a Taipei think-tank backed by the Taiwanese government. Mid-range drones would fill a gap in Taiwan's littoral defense with a cheaper way to strike Chinese forces or weapons from "over-the-horizon" as they approach the island, Barros said. Unlike Ukraine's plains and forests, Taiwan's littoral defense covers a strait notorious for bad winds and volatile sea states, suggesting that Taipei may want its own drone built to withstand poor weather. Instead of air defense systems or supply trucks like in Ukraine or Crimea, Taiwan's mid-range drones would likely target slow-moving vessels transporting troops or weapons, Barros added. "A range of 40 kilometers to 60 kilometers would be very useful for a whole host of different platforms, anything to make it more difficult for the PLA to start getting into Taiwan's territorial waters," he said, referring to the People's Liberation Army. Taiwan's government has said that it plans to produce 100,000 drones a month by 2030. In June, its national defense ministry proposed a $6.6 billion budget to procure over 210,000 domestically produced attack, reconnaissance, and sea drones. It's all part of the island's emerging "hellscape" strategy, which aims to hamper Chinese forces attempting to cross the Taiwan Strait by flooding it with thousands of aerial, surface, and underwater drones. The littoral drills on Saturday, attended by Taiwanese president Lai Ching-te , also featured naval special forces deploying in the island's homegrown M109 Skyship rigid-hull inflatable boats. Taiwan's navy and coast guard launched rapid sorties with four of its older, 170-ton Kuang Hua-6 missile boats and at least one Anping-class patrol vessel — a newer, 600-ton catamaran that can be fitted with anti-ship missiles during wartime. The Han Kuang exercise, which lasts 10 days and 9 nights this year, features island-wide drills to simulate how Taiwanese forces and civilian institutions would respond to Chinese gray-zone tactics and an invasion. items.title: 5 flaws in the ‘augmented work’ myth: What a major Québec survey found
items.summary: We’re being promised a revolution. Artificial intelligence is said to make work both more productive and more enjoyable by freeing us from tedious tasks and allowing us to devote more time to what really matters. This is the narrative of “augmented work.” But what is the reality for people who are already working with AI? To find out, our research team, led by the International Observatory on the Social Impacts of AI and Digital Technology (Obvia), partnered with 11 labor unions representing more than 1.4 million members. Together, we surveyed 4,595 union members in Québec in 2025. Our findings urge us to seriously reconsider the myth that machines universally improve work. Productivity gains less obvious than advertised Let’s start with the flagship promise: productivity. If AI lives up to its promises, its users should be able to work more efficiently. However, among those who use it daily, only 44 per cent report a real gain in productivity. Even more surprisingly, 26 per cent report a loss of efficiency because of the technology. These productivity losses stem in particular from the proliferation of “quick and sloppy” work generated by AI (known as “AI slop”), whose poor quality leads to sometimes significant time losses . This could involve a report that needs to be redone because it does not meet quality standards, information that needs to be verified because it is deemed unreliable, a chain of emails that has become incomprehensible and requires clarification among colleagues, and so on. Adopting AI therefore doesn’t guarantee real benefits. It all depends on the tasks, the context, and the person’s profile. Moreover, AI remains, for now, limited to minor tasks: 75 per cent of users employ it for support or in a secondary role, and only three per cent make it a central part of their work. As many winners as losers The second promise of “augmented work” is a lighter workload. Here again, the picture is mixed. AI does indeed lighten the burden for 46 per cent of respondents. But it increases the burden for nearly one in five (17 per cent) and makes no difference for the remaining third. For example, a paralegal may become more efficient thanks to AI, but ultimately be assigned more cases or tasks, resulting in a heavier workload. Our data shows the same ambivalence regarding workplace stress. AI reduces stress for 28 per cent of respondents and increases it for another 28 per cent, an even split. A college professor sums up this tension: “Tools are evolving so quickly that we don’t have time to keep up with the changes. This is anxiety-provoking and discouraging.” In other words, AI doesn’t improve work across the board, it reshapes it. And depending on the sector, profession or age of the employee, this reshaping can be for better or for worse. Augmented work: It depends on who you ask This is undoubtedly the most important finding of our study: the benefits of AI are not distributed randomly; they follow the existing fault lines in the labour market. Professionals and college graduates are among the biggest winners. They report using AI independently, becoming more productive and participating fully in decision-making. At the other end of the spectrum, technical, industrial and service workers are more often forced to use AI. They report experiencing greater algorithmic surveillance and seeing fewer of its benefits. The perception of increased productivity clearly illustrates this divide: 55 per cent of post-graduate degree holders consider themselves more productive thanks to AI, compared to only 22 per cent of high school graduates. À lire aussi : Why the real test of Canada’s AI strategy is in university classrooms Lack of oversight and communication There are two things almost everyone laments. First, a lack of oversight within organizations: only 24 per cent of respondents say their organization has a policy or other mechanism governing AI use. Second, the rollout is anything but transparent and democratic: barely 12 per cent say they were consulted before deployment, and only 26 per cent believe their organization is transparent about its use of AI. As a result, only 35 per cent trust their employer on its AI initiatives. Fear of job replacement Nearly one in five people (18 per cent) fear for their job because of AI. This concern increases with age and is significantly more pronounced among those working in manufacturing and services, as well as among those with fewer educational credentials. These results contrast with most major forecasting studies that predict that skilled office jobs are the most at risk from AI. This discrepancy between the models’ predictions and the fears people actually feel is worth examining: it serves as a reminder that technological anxiety often takes root where people already feel most vulnerable. Looking at the facts What should we take away from this? That “augmented work” is not a lie, but an incomplete narrative. For some workers, often the most skilled, AI is indeed a welcome support tool that they use on their own initiative. For many others, it is a source of pressure, reduced autonomy, surveillance or job insecurity. At a time when organizations are facing challenges related to skills, qualifications, staff shortages and innovation, the issues raised by AI in the workplace must be put back at the centre of decision-making: AI alone cannot be the solution. Taking the time to discuss AI with all affected staff can lead to much greater results: the more people are trained, engaged and truly involved, the more tangible the benefits become, and the more we can prevent AI from ultimately undermining the very work it claims to improve in the absence of collective thinking about how it’s used. “Tools are evolving so quickly that we don’t have time to keep up with the changes. This is anxiety-provoking and discouraging.”

items.title: I've been a flight attendant for years. Here are the 5 mistakes I always see travelers make.
items.summary: As a flight attendant, I've seen passengers make some common flying mistakes in the airport and on the plane. YakobchukOlena/Getty Images I've worked as a flight attendant for several years and have seen passengers make many mistakes. Don't leave the airport during a long delay, but do consider paying extra to choose your seat. Get to the airport at least two hours before a domestic flight and three before international ones. I became a flight attendant in 2022, and the job has made me a better traveler. It's also made me a more frequent one, and I prioritize taking vacations almost every month. Last year alone, I flew on over 250 flights. Along the way, I've learned some great travel tips and witnessed some mishaps in airports and on planes. Whether I'm flying as a passenger or as a crewmember, these are the most common mistakes I see travelers make: Failing to get to the airport early enough Don't wait until the last minute to get to the airport. Grant Faint/Getty Images I often see passengers miss their flights because they didn't give themselves enough time to get to and through the airport. It's worth following what might be a golden rule of air travel: Get to the airport two hours before departure for domestic flights and three hours before for international ones. People often ask me what the latest time they can get to the airport is because they don't want to wait around. But in my opinion, trying to arrive as late as possible isn't worth the risk. Unexpected situations can arise —  parking could be challenging to find, the check-in counter could be understaffed, TSA could be backed up, or your gate could change. Regardless, I'd rather have the extra time to relax at the airport before my flight. If the day goes smoothly, you can use those extra hours to refill your water bottle, stop by the restroom, grab a coffee, and buy snacks for the plane . Also, remember that departure time is different from door-closure time. Boarding typically ends around 15 minutes before departure. After the aircraft door is shut, the gate agents won't reopen it for you. Overindulging at the airport bar Don't get me wrong — when I'm traveling for fun instead of work, I also love a pre-departure drink. Just be careful not to overdo it. The FAA strictly prohibits airlines from allowing intoxicated passengers to board a plane. A big reason is that intoxicated passengers will likely have trouble following crewmembers' instructions, especially in an emergency. Alcohol could also cause a passenger to become belligerent, which is harder to control in the air than on the ground. If the crew notices that a passenger appears to be intoxicated during boarding, they are legally required to report it. From there, a specially trained airline employee called a Complaint Resolution Official (CRO) will usually come on board to assess the passenger. If the CRO confirms the passenger to be intoxicated, the FAA requires them to be removed from the flight. This is the most common reason I've had to have passengers kicked off my flights . Leaving the airport during a long delay Even if your flight is delayed a few hours, you may want to hang tight. gahsoon/Getty Images Did you know flights can "un-delay" ? It's rare, but it happens. Airlines try to avoid this by delaying flights in small increments at a time. Sometimes, though, a solution could come up that reverses the delay. For example, the airline could locate a replacement plane for your flight, a different crew could become available to work, or the weather could clear up faster than expected. If you live far from the airport and see that your flight is delayed, you might see it as an opportunity to arrive later. If you live nearby, you might even take this as an opportunity to go home. However, regardless of how long your flight is delayed, you should remain close enough to the airport to get to your gate with little notice. If the delay reverses and you're not there, the plane will leave without you. Not securing your seat in advance If you don't select your seat in advance, you are not guaranteed to be seated with the people you're traveling with. This is true even if you booked the flights on the same reservation — and even if you're traveling with kids . If you need to be seated next to your travel buddy, you should select your seats in advance. Even if you're traveling alone, I still recommend choosing your seat. If you don't, you'll get everyone else's leftovers, which is usually a middle seat. In addition, if you have a tight connection, it might be worth paying for a seat closer to the front. When I fly as a passenger, I always pick my seat. I want the window seat on short flights because I like the view, and the aisle for long-hauls so I can get up without disturbing anyone else. Some airlines will let you choose your seat for free, but others will charge a fee. Regardless, I believe it's worth it. Not wiping down your seat before you sit in it Cleaning procedures may vary across flights, airlines, and airports. Alexander Spatari/Getty Images Cleaning procedures vary across airlines, but generally, I've seen the process between flights be pretty minimal. Think about how quickly you sometimes see flights boarding after watching the previous passengers deplane. Depending on the airline or even the airport, cleaning might primarily consist of picking up visible trash and vacuuming. Considering I see bare feet and dirty diapers on the tray tables almost daily, I never travel without my own disinfecting wipes. In my opinion, the only way to truly guarantee your seat has been sanitized is to do it yourself. Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: I went from wedding DJ to Meta engineer, then was laid off after 13 years. My last years there brought constant change.
items.summary: Henry Chen spent more than 13 years at Facebook and Meta before being laid off in May. Henry Chen Henry Chen went from wedding DJ to Meta engineer before being laid off after 13 years. He taught himself to code, rising from conference room technician to tech lead. Chen shared how he's navigated his job search since being laid off in May. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Henry Chen, a former Meta tech lead who was laid off in May. He's 38 and lives in the San Francisco Bay Area. The following has been edited for length and clarity. After I left college, I worked as a DJ for a few years, taught myself to code, and eventually found my way to Facebook. I started at Facebook as a contractor in 2012, and then worked my way up into a full-time engineering role. After more than 13 years with the company, I was laid off in May . I'm grateful for everything I learned during my time at Facebook, later Meta. Overall, it was a very positive experience. But after the company's major layoffs in late 2022 and early 2023, things started to change. Before then, I felt our teams had the resources to build ambitious projects. Following the layoffs, the focus seemed to shift toward doing more with less . About a year and a half later, the focus seemed to shift again, with a renewed emphasis on building. Between leadership changes and shifting priorities, it became harder to know where my team was headed and what we should prioritize. The ongoing changes were especially difficult for me because I was on paternity leave from August 2025 through near the end of the year. By the time I returned to work, the company was using AI much more extensively, there had been team and leadership shifts, and it took me some time to get reacclimated. After being away for four months, it felt like the whole company had changed. On May 20, I learned that I'd lost my job — and that many of my colleagues had lost theirs, too. I started looking for work before the layoff — then stopped once it happened The layoffs themselves weren't entirely surprising because the company had already confirmed they were coming. I was still surprised to be affected, even though I'd felt more uneasy about this round than the previous ones. During earlier layoffs, I felt relatively secure because I believed my work was critical to the company. This time, nothing specific gave me a sign I would be affected, but the situation just felt different. In the weeks leading up to my layoff, I'd already started looking for new roles . I was feeling a little more anxious about the possibility of losing my job, and I'd also been doing some introspection, thinking it might be time for a new chapter in my career. Once I was laid off, my approach changed. Meta provided a generous severance package that reflected my roughly 10 years as a full-time employee. That financial cushion, combined with the start of my kids' summer break, made it feel like the right time to take a break. I spent time with my family, tried to relax, and planned to resume my job search after about a month. Business Insider is speaking with workers who've found themselves at a corporate crossroads — whether due to a layoff, resignation, job search, or shifting workplace expectations. Share your story by filling out this form . From DJ to Meta engineer When I resumed my job search, I found myself reflecting on my career — and which types of roles to pursue. In the early 2010s, I was pursuing a degree at San Jose State University . I planned to go into education and become a teacher, but I left school before earning my degree for personal reasons. Before leaving school, I started working as a DJ and continued for a while after, but I eventually began looking for a different career path. I came across an AV engineering contract role that involved inspecting conference rooms. My background working with audio and video equipment made me a good fit. Henry Chen

  • He taught himself to code, rising from conference room technician to tech lead.

I started at Facebook as a contractor in 2012, and then worked my way up into a full-time engineering role. After more than 13 years with the company, I was laid off in May.

I'm grateful for everything I learned during my time at Facebook, later Meta. Overall, it was a very positive experience. But after the company's major layoffs in late 2022 and early 2023, things started to change.

Before then, I felt our teams had the resources to build ambitious projects. Following the layoffs, the focus seemed to shift toward doing more with less. About a year and a half later, the focus seemed to shift again, with a renewed emphasis on building. Between leadership changes and shifting priorities, it became harder to know where my team was headed and what we should prioritize.

The ongoing changes were especially difficult for me because I was on paternity leave from August 2025 through near the end of the year. By the time I returned to work, the company was using AI much more extensively, there had been team and leadership shifts, and it took me some time to get reacclimated. After being away for four months, it felt like the whole company had changed.

On May 20, I learned that I'd lost my job — and that many of my colleagues had lost theirs, too.

I started looking for work before the layoff — then stopped once it happened

The layoffs themselves weren't entirely surprising because the company had already confirmed they were coming. I was still surprised to be affected, even though I'd felt more uneasy about this round than the previous ones.

During earlier layoffs, I felt relatively secure because I believed my work was critical to the company. This time, nothing specific gave me a sign I would be affected, but the situation just felt different.

In the weeks leading up to my layoff, I'd already started looking for new roles. I was feeling a little more anxious about the possibility of losing my job, and I'd also been doing some introspection, thinking it might be time for a new chapter in my career.

Once I was laid off, my approach changed. Meta provided a generous severance package that reflected my roughly 10 years as a full-time employee. That financial cushion, combined with the start of my kids' summer break, made it feel like the right time to take a break. I spent time with my family, tried to relax, and planned to resume my job search after about a month.

From DJ to Meta engineer

When I resumed my job search, I found myself reflecting on my career — and which types of roles to pursue.

In the early 2010s, I was pursuing a degree at San Jose State University. I planned to go into education and become a teacher, but I left school before earning my degree for personal reasons. Before leaving school, I started working as a DJ and continued for a while after, but I eventually began looking for a different career path.

From there, Facebook grew quickly, and my role grew with it. Within a few years, I progressed from inspecting conference rooms as a technician to tackling more advanced work, including building out conference rooms. In 2015, I landed a full-time operations engineer role managing the collaboration technologies used in Facebook's conference rooms.

Around 2017, Facebook's growth accelerated further, and so did the number of conference rooms. I started experimenting with Python, despite having very little coding experience, to help solve the problems presented while scaling. I wrote a script that made it much faster to update conference room technology, and it changed the direction of my career.

Over the next several years, I transitioned into a software engineering role focused on the technology behind Meta's conference rooms, eventually becoming a tech lead.

I'm working with a coach to help with my job search

When I resumed my job search in June, I found myself split between a few different paths: roles in the collaboration technology space, where I'd spent much of my career, broader IT roles at smaller companies, and software engineering opportunities, where I could continue building on the coding skills I'd developed over the past decade.

I hadn't interviewed for a job in 10 years, which is a long time in the tech industry. So before diving into applications, I decided to brush up on software engineering interview topics and identify any gaps in my skill set.

While I'd spent years building software at Meta, many of the tools and systems I worked on were unique to the company. To prepare for my next role, I'm strengthening my understanding of industry-standard system design by designing and building a software system from the ground up. items.title: Traveling with just a backpack taught me that I don't need special clothes to exercise. I wear the same outfit for all my workouts.
items.summary: The author travels all over the world, and packs one quick-dry, breathable shirt, a pair of shorts, and two sports bras for every trip. She borrows equipment when needed, including a Taekwondo uniform. Courtesy of Catherine Work Traveling with only a backpack taught me that most workouts don't require special clothes or gear. Renting or borrowing equipment has let me try sports around the world without spending a lot. Focusing on movement instead of appearances has made exercising while traveling much easier. One unexpected lesson I learned from traveling with just a backpack is that you can't make excuses if you want to stay active. If you spend time looking for the perfect outfit, the best gear, or the right location, you'll end up with a long list of reasons why you can't exercise. "I don't have the right clothes to go to yoga class ," one of my family members said this week when I invited her to a free session at the local recreation center. We were both vacationing with only a backpack's worth of clothes. She skipped the class, and I went in the same outfit I'd already worn for biking, walking, and pickleball that day. As long as I feel comfortable and safe, I'll say yes to almost any exercise while I'm traveling . Living out of a single backpack for months at a time has completely changed how I think about staying healthy. I was inspired to adopt this mindset in my early 20s while living in a rural village in Cameroon. My only options for exercise were running through the jungle and carrying buckets of drinking water from the well to my house. Since then, I've realized that if I want to take care of my body in different environments and situations, I have to be willing to work with whatever conditions I have. The author travels all over, often with just one backpack. Courtesy of Catherine Work I realized that most workouts can be done in the same outfit I pack one quick-dry, breathable shirt, a pair of shorts, and two sports bras for every trip. I wear the same waterproof trail running shoes whether I'm hiking, playing pickleball , or walking around a new city. Sun protection is just as important. A bandana keeps the sun off my neck while also holding back my hair, and I pack lightweight sun gloves that double as cycling gloves. That same outfit even works for many water sports when I want extra sun coverage. Sometimes people arrive at yoga classes wearing expensive matching sets. I'm just proud that I figured out how to find and sign up for a workout in a new country . Any self-consciousness I might feel about my clothes disappears as soon as class begins. Besides, the people I meet while traveling will probably never see me again. While I will run in the rain, sun, or snow, I have limits. I don't feel bad about skipping an intense three-day trek because I didn't pack heavy hiking boots. Traveling light means accepting a few trade-offs, and I'm comfortable with that. I borrow or rent gear instead of buying it Some sports also have specialized equipment, which can get expensive, but you can rent or borrow whatever you need if you're resourceful. I've been handed a karate uniform in Seoul, climbing shoes for bouldering in Hanoi, a surfboard in Peru, and a helmet for windsurfing in Thessaloniki. Buying and hauling sports equipment around the world would be expensive, heavy, and impractical. By not owning much gear, I feel freer to try new activities wherever I go. Sports that require me to purchase lots of expensive equipment, like scuba diving or skiing, simply aren't a priority for me. When I'm booking accommodations , I look for places with bikes or a yoga mat. If I'm visiting friends, I'll happily ask to borrow whatever equipment we need for an activity. I also benefit from having a boyfriend who's the same size as me, which effectively doubles my workout wardrobe whenever we're together. Traveling light reminds me that working out should be simple Exercise should be easy and affordable. Wearing the same outfit for nearly every workout reminds me that I'm there to care for my body, not to impress anyone. I spend less time packing, shopping, and deciding what to wear, and more time actually moving. Living for months out of a backpack has taught me that I don't need perfect conditions to stay active. I just need to show up. Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: As AI guzzles water and energy, we are already facing a choice: datacentres or homes? | John Harris
items.summary: Whitehall wants to triple their number in the UK. Yet in Slough, I saw the impact they’re having on communities Amid headlines about the UK’s drought , Europe’s wildfires and impossible global temperatures, it was 28C when I arrived in Slough last Monday. I was there to look around Slough Trading Estate, a place that might once have conjured up images of the TV comedy The Office , many of whose laughs came at the expense of this overgrown patch of suburbia, 20-odd miles west of London. But these days, this area of town – an incongruous mixture of old-school businesses such as Mr Clutch and Angling Direct, and vast, metal-clad leviathans that look like something pulled from JG Ballard – has become a byword for the constant expansion of datacentres, those hulking symbols of the vast computing power that big tech now requires, not least because of the ever-more complex workings of artificial intelligence. items.title: Reading the Room Perfectly, Donald Trump Becomes Greatest Defender of Data Centers
items.summary: It’s no secret that data centers have become a massive sore point for a vast swathe of the American electorate. Poll after poll has found that the facilities are immensely unpopular, a key bipartisan issue that could prove significant during this year’s midterm elections. The situation has become so heated there have already been at least 37 arrests stemming from protests against the projects this year. Broadly speaking, critics take issue with the sheer amount of space data centers take up, how much air and noise pollution they generate, concerns that they’re driving up electricity prices — all while barely making a difference job creation. Moratoriums on new data center projects like the New York governor Kathy Hochul imposed last month are currently a bipartisan slam dunk . Yet in his great political wisdom, president Donald Trump is siding firmly with villains of the day. “I saw Texas the other day sort of is against data centers,” he told Punchbowl News in a new interview . “I think it’s a mistake.” Trump was likely referring to the gold rush-like scramble to construct new data centers in the Lone Star State suffering a brutal collision with reality . Last week, governor Greg Abbott announced a pause on new approvals on the projects to save Texas’ already shaky power grid from collapsing in on itself. The president gushed over data centers being some of the “most incredible buildings I’ve ever seen” — while wind mills with far smaller footprints are “ ugly losers ” — and argued that they’re “tremendously important for the economics” and “income.” Trump went as far as to argue that data centers “could be bigger than oil,” raging that we “can’t let China beat us at this.” The outburst builds on a sense that Trump is increasingly a political outsider in the US. His approval ratings have hit historic lows , showing widespread disillusionment with the Iran war, fluctuating gas prices, and a growing affordability crisis. Trump has maintained what’s been criticized as a “ too cozy relationship ” with the tech industry. In return, AI tech leaders, many of whom have made sizeable donations to Trump’s political efforts, have enjoyed a largely regulation-free policy environment. The reality is that the benefits of data centers are dicey. Critics argue that the resource-hogging facilities only line the pockets of a few multibillionaires and most of the times aren’t accompanied by an economic boom or spike in employment in places where they’re being built. Instead, researchers warn they’re leading to a significant rise in greenhouse gas emissions , particularly in Texas, where many are using gas-burning backup generators to stay online . Meanwhile, those who refuse contracts for their land be used to construct new data centers are being hailed as folk heroes . Naturally, Trump took full credit for the AI boom in the US. “And if we turn off on data centers, we turn off on AI,” he told Punchbowl . “We are leading because of me. We’re leading AI. Remember this. I came up with an idea that was a great idea. Nobody thought it was serious.” More on data centers: The Number of Regular People Being Arrested for Protesting Data Centers Is Astounding The post Reading the Room Perfectly, Donald Trump Becomes Greatest Defender of Data Centers appeared first on Futurism .

items.title: Mount Toba eruption doesn't seem like it could nearly kill our species
items.summary: Mount Toba was the biggest volcanic eruption in the last 2.6 million years, and some have suggested it nearly wiped out humanity. Around 74,000 years ago, a caldera on what is now Sumatra emptied thousands of cubic kilometers of magma in about two weeks, roughly a thousand times more than Mount Pinatubo spewed out in 1991. “People thought it might have caused massive cooling of the planet, and hence threatened the survival of our ancestors,” says Jinheum Park, a geoscientist at Johannes Gutenberg University in Mainz, Germany. Park and his colleagues went looking for the records of that catastrophe in the mud taken from the bottom of a small crater lake on the Kenya-Tanzania border. They found instead that the effects of the Mount Toba eruption lasted under two years and amounted to perhaps half a degree of cooling. Muddy calendars Volcanic eruptions inject sulfur dioxide into the stratosphere, where it becomes a haze of tiny droplets that reflect sunlight back into space. Bigger eruptions eject more sulfur dioxide and, in principle, cause more cooling. But this trend stops working when the eruption exceeds a certain magnitude. “Bigger sulfate aerosols settle quickly, because they are heavier,” Park explains. This quick settling makes them less effective in scattering incoming solar radiation. Read full article Comments

items.title: I work from home, and our family helps with childcare. We're still putting our daughter in part-time day care.
items.summary: The author's mother-in-law and mother both chip in with childcare. However, they have decided that part-time day care would still be helpful. Courtesy of Riana Ang-Canning Both my mother and mother-in-law help a few days a week with childcare for my 18-month-old daughter. While I'm grateful, they're not here as often as I need to get all my work done. We've decided to enroll my daughter in part-time childcare, even though it's expensive. As a stay-at-home, work-from-home mom, I am primarily responsible for my 18-month-old daughter's childcare during the workweek. Even with childcare help from my mom and mother-in-law, it's still hard to find time to get all of my work done on top of childcare and household tasks. I'm so lucky that my work is flexible and that I get to spend so much time with my daughter. And I'm even luckier that my mom and mother-in-law help us with childcare three mornings per week. But after a few months of our current childcare situation, I was still finding it difficult to get everything done. And on days when I was solely responsible for childcare, dog walks, household chores, and squeezing my work into nap and bedtime, I was absolutely drained. And so, we decided to enroll our daughter in part-time day care to help lighten my load. She'll be starting next week, and while it will be a big adjustment, I'm confident we're making the right decision. Day care will give me more consistent hours to get my work done I am so grateful that we have family members who are willing and able to help with childcare. My mom and mother-in-law come over three mornings per week, babysitting my daughter for two to three hours each time. While that is helpful, it's hard for me to get much done in that time. In addition to work, I'm also using those two to three hours to walk our dog, prep lunch , do any necessary household chores, and sometimes even to shower. The hours and days are also not consistent. Almost every week, we need to swap days around to accommodate someone's schedule. There isn't a strict start time, so I never know exactly when my mom or mother-in-law will arrive. Both grandmothers also regularly go on vacation, meaning some weeks or months they can't provide childcare at all. The author believes there are more pros than cons to enrolling her daughter in day care. items.title: We wore shorts to the office. Our boss didn't.
items.summary: BI This post originally appeared in the BI Today newsletter. You can sign up for Business Insider's daily newsletter here . Free the knee Shorts at the office . Appropriate or not? It's a heated and long-running debate across much of corporate America, one that Instagram boss Adam Mosseri recently planted his flag in . He said he was "pro" shorts in the workplace, with caveats. "Not all shorts are created equal," he said. Somewhat dangerously, he added that not everyone can "pull them off." We decided to test how summer shorts look in our own office. On Friday, 10 Business Insider journalists, myself included, wore shorts to our New York headquarters — much to the chagrin of Editor in Chief Jamie Heller. "I would never," Jamie said, explaining that she works better in business attire. "The one time I wore black jeans to the office, on Christmas Eve, I immediately regretted it," she said. This newsletter's weekday writer, Dan DeFrancesco, refused to partake in Friday's leg-baring festivities. "I like wearing shorts as much as the next guy, but we live in a society with rules," he said. "Imagine being on a deadline, and you look over and catch a glimpse of my hairy man thighs. It's a lose-lose situation." (TMI, we know.) We wanted a larger sample size on this hot-button issue. So we posed the question on LinkedIn . More than 7,000 people have voted so far in our poll, and the knees are losing. As of Friday afternoon, 55% said shorts weren't appropriate, versus 20% who said they were. Another 25% went with the less definitive option: It depends. This is, of course, a LinkedIn poll, and not peer-reviewed research. But the comments featured lively insights into what readers consider suitable office attire in 2026. Some proposed a shorts hierarchy. Chinos? Sure. Basketball shorts? Absolutely not. Then there are skirts, which are already acceptable, so why shouldn't appropriately tailored shorts get the same treatment? Where you work matters, too. Shorts at a startup or fashion company may barely register. Somewhere more buttoned-up? That's a different story. One reader suggested a 90-degree rule. When the temperature rises above 90 degrees, shorts are fair game, he says. Though anyone who's shivered under frigid office air conditioning in the summer knows the irony there. I've found many of the Gen Zers in our newsroom are jazzed by shorts in the office. Personally, as an elder millennial, I can't get on board. I tried it. I wrote this newsletter in the office while wearing shorts and felt woefully underdressed in a way I have only ever felt once before . Don't worry, Jamie, it won't happen again. Shorts at the office. Appropriate or not?

It's a heated and long-running debate across much of corporate America, one that Instagram boss Adam Mosseri recently planted his flag in. He said he was "pro" shorts in the workplace, with caveats.

"Not all shorts are created equal," he said. Somewhat dangerously, he added that not everyone can "pull them off."

We decided to test how summer shorts look in our own office. On Friday, 10 Business Insider journalists, myself included, wore shorts to our New York headquarters — much to the chagrin of Editor in Chief Jamie Heller.

"I would never," Jamie said, explaining that she works better in business attire. "The one time I wore black jeans to the office, on Christmas Eve, I immediately regretted it," she said.

This newsletter's weekday writer, Dan DeFrancesco, refused to partake in Friday's leg-baring festivities. "I like wearing shorts as much as the next guy, but we live in a society with rules," he said. "Imagine being on a deadline, and you look over and catch a glimpse of my hairy man thighs. It's a lose-lose situation." (TMI, we know.)

We wanted a larger sample size on this hot-button issue. So we posed the question on LinkedIn. More than 7,000 people have voted so far in our poll, and the knees are losing.

As of Friday afternoon, 55% said shorts weren't appropriate, versus 20% who said they were. Another 25% went with the less definitive option: It depends.

This is, of course, a LinkedIn poll, and not peer-reviewed research. But the comments featured lively insights into what readers consider suitable office attire in 2026.

Some proposed a shorts hierarchy. Chinos? Sure. Basketball shorts? Absolutely not. Then there are skirts, which are already acceptable, so why shouldn't appropriately tailored shorts get the same treatment?

Where you work matters, too. Shorts at a startup or fashion company may barely register. Somewhere more buttoned-up? That's a different story.

One reader suggested a 90-degree rule. When the temperature rises above 90 degrees, shorts are fair game, he says. Though anyone who's shivered under frigid office air conditioning in the summer knows the irony there.

I've found many of the Gen Zers in our newsroom are jazzed by shorts in the office. Personally, as an elder millennial, I can't get on board. I tried it. I wrote this newsletter in the office while wearing shorts and felt woefully underdressed in a way I have only ever felt once before.

Don't worry, Jamie, it won't happen again.

items.summary: Britain's employment courts saw 39 percent more claims in the year through March 2026, many written with ChatGPT or Grok. The backlog jumped 55 percent to 64,000 unresolved cases, with AI-generated filings often running hundreds of pages and citing fabricated laws. The Economist calls it a "tragedy of the commons, AI edition," where workers with real grievances wait longer for justice. items.title: We saw Beta Technologies' autonomous aircraft for the battlefield. Meet the MV250.
items.summary: Cargo is loaded into the nose of the MV250. Pete Syme/Business Insider Beta Technologies unveiled an autonomous military aircraft at the Farnborough Airshow. The MV250 can carry a ton of cargo up to 250 nautical miles. Air taxi firms are becoming increasingly attractive for defense purposes. Uncrewed aircraft are becoming more important to militaries, and defense departments are increasingly looking to air-taxi companies for help. Beta Technologies unveiled the MV250, an autonomous hybrid-electric cargo aircraft, at the Farnborough Airshow in July. Business Insider was there to see why the company believes it could be a valuable tool for the future battlefield. Beta initially focused on civil electric aircraft. But as militaries seek new ways to move supplies amid increasingly autonomous warfare, Beta has adapted its technology for a new customer. The MV250 can take off and land vertically, fly without a pilot aboard, and carry up to a ton of cargo into dangerous areas. Here's what it's like, and why it matters. Beta Technologies is one of several firms building air taxis — electric aircraft that can take off and land vertically. Beta's Alia-250 eVTOL during a test flight in 2023. Tiffany Hagler-Geard/Bloomberg via Getty Images These eVTOLs operate like helicopters but make very little noise. So, they wouldn't annoy residents when flying over cities. Beta is also building an electric aircraft that takes off and lands conventionally, known as a CTOL. Earlier this year, Beta deployed its all-electric ALIA CTOL aircraft during NATO Exercise Aurora 26 in Sweden. It then adapted that technology into a military aircraft, the MV250. Pete Syme/Business Insider It is a hybrid-electric aircraft that can take off vertically and fly autonomously. "Why do we all want autonomy? I'm a pilot. No pilot wants to see their job go away," said Gen. Jim McConville, a former chief of staff of the US Army and a Beta board member. "But what we want to do is give commanders the ability to go into situations at extremely high risk." For example, in Ukraine , aerial drones and ground robots are increasingly being used for logistics missions that have become too dangerous for soldiers. Ukrainian officials have said that they want machines to eventually handle 100% of battlefield logistics amid a broader push to replace humans with robotics wherever possible. Instead of carrying pilots or passengers, it can transport up to a ton of cargo. Taylor Rains/Business Insider The MV250's nose opens to reveal a cargo bay capable of carrying up to 2,000 pounds of equipment, medical supplies, munitions, or other critical cargo. Beta says it can take that payload to destinations within a 250-nautical-mile tactical radius, roughly 288 miles, and return to base. Beta says hybrid-electric power means it can fly faster and farther than a helicopter. Taylor Rains/Business Insider A turbogenerator developed with GE Aerospace produces electricity for the MV250's motors. As well as the 1,300-nautical-mile repositioning range — when it isn't carrying a payload — Beta says it can generate power on the ground for equipment such as radar, antennas, and other vehicles. Beta says its bonded-composite fuselage could speed up production. Taylor Rains/Business Insider The MV250's fuselage is bonded together rather than held with conventional fasteners. "That allows us to make this in a panini press, basically," Clark said. "You can make it inexpensively and meet the demands of the military." Beta says manufacturing cycle times could be measured in hours rather than months. It has also designed the aircraft without gearboxes, hydraulics, or articulating rotors, systems that can add maintenance demands. During earlier military exercises with Beta's all-electric aircraft, Clark said the company sent one maintainer and one pilot — and "the maintainer was bored." Beta thinks military demand could develop faster than the air-taxi market. Taylor Rains/Business Insider Beta developed the technology behind the MV250 for civilian electric aircraft, but Clark said defense customers may adopt vertical-lift technology sooner. "Near-term defense, I think, will take a pace in front of civil in vertical lift, and then civil will overtake that," he said. Defense dominated this year's Farnborough Airshow as governments are growing more concerned about security. Andrew Matthews/PA Images via Getty Images Defense companies made up about half of the roughly 1,600 exhibitors at this year's airshow, up from the roughly 40% share they usually represent. The event drew over 140,000 visitors, a 41% increase on the last edition in 2024. The shift reflects a scramble to rearm as wars have reshaped military priorities, including the need for cheaper drones , autonomous systems, and new ways to move supplies. NATO allies have also committed to raising defense and security-related spending to 5% of GDP by 2035, after President Donald Trump pressed them to spend more. items.title: Summerween is in full swing with candy brands leaning harder into the trend
items.summary: Halloween candy is hitting shelves earlier as the Summerween trend goes mainstream. Brandon Bell/Getty Images Spooky Season is earlier on the calendar, with Halloween products hitting stores in the summer. Candy brands are all-in on the shift trend, building on promising sales results from recent years. Candy corn is arriving earlier than ever, Brach's says, and new treats are launching soon. Halloween is getting creepier. The last few years have seen the start of Spooky Season creep earlier on the calendar, with candy and merchandise hitting retail shelves a full three months ahead of the actual holiday. "It's hard to tell if any of this is actually needle-moving, or if it's just a testing ground for the actual Halloween period. But it's definitely something I see in the stores a bit more," Mizuho analyst David Bellinger told Business Insider. Summerween, as it's often called, has been growing for more than a decade now. The trend may trace its roots to a 2012 episode of Gravity Falls in which the Halloween-loving characters go trick-or-treating in June. Retailers soon jumped in , led by the likes of craft store Michael's and off-price retailers like T.J. Maxx and Home Goods, with Walmart launching a line of "Summer Frights" decor last year. This year, candy brands are all-in on the shift. "Candy corn is the Summerween trend — like, this is what really started it all," Matthew Escalante, vice president of Brach's and seasonal candies at Ferrara, told Business Insider. Escalante said customers see their first purchase of candy corn as marking the start of fall. The company said 17% of candy corn purchases are made before Labor Day, citing Circana data. "This year we've seen candy corn creep out even earlier, which we're excited about," he said. "Our sales are up pretty substantially versus this time year ago on candy corn due to getting out there earlier." Hershey CEO Kirk Tanner said on a July 30 earnings call that this year's "Summerween" sales were already off to a strong start. "Our frontline sales team is really dialed up this year," he said. "We feel good about where we're going to be." Hershey chief growth and marketing officer, Stacy Taffet, told Business Insider's CMO Insider that one way the company is keeping spirits up through the long slog to October is by dividing the time into distinct micro-seasons that feature different brands, products, and price points. A survey last month from Morning Consult and Hershey found two thirds of US parents had bought Halloween candy or snacks during the summer in recent years. Hershey competitor Mars also launched its Halloween offerings in July with a hundred-day countdown to October 31. "Halloween is becoming America's longest seasonal shopping occasion," the company said in marketing materials for the kickoff. Escalante said Brach's has several candy corn variations in the works to keep customer interest from fading through the long march to the end of October, plus offerings from other Ferrara brands. "We have our new Spooky Graveyard, which gives us a little more of a Halloween flavor — which is going to have a bunch of shapes like tombstones and ghosts and bats — which we're really excited to launch this year," he said. "While candy corn is the lead and the first one out, we have a full portfolio that does well across the Halloween season." The pull-forward isn't limited to the candy aisles. Warehouse clubs like Costco and Sam's Club are usually some of the first to roll out seasonal products, but this year seemed to push even earlier, with costumes and skeletons sharing the floor with Independence Day hot dogs and fireworks. At Costco, a 5-foot-tall, 9-foot-wide skeleton decoration was available in the first week of July, and Home Depot is already taking orders for its viral 2-gallon "Boo Bucket" after selling through supplies last year. "I looked for them last year. Nobody had them," Bellinger said. "The store associates would tell me that hey, you're the sixth person who's come in today and you can't find a bucket." America's 250th birthday is also helping drive the shift, according to Cracker Barrel CEO Julie Felss Masino, who is stepping down August 10. "It's been so popular that actually we had to pull Halloween up, because we've been running out of this American Heritage product. So, Halloween actually hit the floor for us this past week and that's actually off to a great start as well," she said during an earnings call in early June. It's hard to say where Halloween's calendar creep will stop, but it's not likely to encroach on Easter. "We're not necessarily trying to get into May with this thing, but it's more about how do we get to a greater breadth of stores," Escalante said. Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: An Ivy League whisperer shares her best advice for wealthy parents to get their kids into an elite college
items.summary: Drusilla Blackman is the founder of Deans of Admissions. Deans of Admissions Drusilla Blackman knows how wealthy parents can get their kids into elite colleges. The admissions guru says to ignore the neighbors, make time to chat, and don't run the show. The former Harvard and Columbia dean of admissions said children need to figure out who they are. Many wealthy parents obsess about getting their kids into a great college, believing it will set them up for life. Drusilla Blackman specializes in helping them achieve that goal. Blackman, a former dean of admissions at Harvard and later Columbia, is the founder of Deans of Admissions, a group of former admissions executives who advise families on how to land their children at top-flight universities in the US and Britain. She spoke to Business Insider this week about how wealthy parents can inadvertently sabotage their kids' chances at a coveted spot in an Ivy League-level institution, and how they can maximize their prospects instead. Ignore the person next door Blackman said one of the biggest mistakes that affluent families make is that they "listen to their neighbors." Wealthy parents who have "never been inside the process" wrongly believe the couple next door, because they managed to get their kids into an exceptional school, " have the answers that they should apply to their children," she said. But no two kids have the same personalities, interests, and abilities, meaning that what worked for one family almost certainly won't work for another, Blackman said. Make time for talking Blackman said the " best piece of advice " she has for affluent parents is to "create as many opportunities as possible just to talk as a family." Parents who sit down for meals with their children and carve out quality time with them can learn about their interests, successes, and struggles, and vice versa. "You'd be amazed at how seen everyone in the family feels over activities like that," Blackman said. She also suggested parents take their kids to their workplaces so they can see what they do every day, and learn to appreciate the relationship between work and money. Kids must learn who they are Warren Buffett famously advises wealthy parents to give their kids "enough to do anything, but not enough to do nothing." Blackman agreed that giving too much money, too soon, to your children is a bad idea , as it can stop them from learning about themselves. "Success in any field is really a result of knowing yourself inside, how you feel about and respond to situations, and what's important to you ," Blackman said. "You cannot know that if everything is given to you. You never take the time to learn those things." Blackman said that when she was choosing between two exceptional candidates as a dean of admissions, the deciding factor was often "depth of character." She favored candidates who were more self-reflective , more in touch and thoughtful about who they were and who they would become, she said. Blackman said she rejected many applicants who were "perfect on paper" because they didn't strike her as real, "just kind of manufactured to seem like ideal candidates." "Authenticity counts for a lot ," she said. Blackman recalled advising a family who wanted their son to attend Harvard, but he wasn't spending his time doing Model UN or taking part in the kinds of clubs that typically support an Ivy League application. Instead, he "took great pleasure in composing on the piano," Blackman said. His parents complained to her that his piano playing wasn't academic enough and might stop him from getting into Harvard, but Blackman told them that colleges value passions . She recognized that to him, music was a "way for him to communicate what he was feeling inside to others." Blackman helped him articulate the importance of his piano playing in essays, and the final result was "moving" and "elegant," showing who he was as an individual, she said. "He ultimately wound up at Harvard because of his essay and his piano, and what it taught him," she said. Parents don't always know best Blackman warned parents not to micromanage their kids' lives to get them into a certain college, as that approach is often ineffective and can backfire. She said they shouldn't decide where they want their child to be in 10 or 20 years, but instead "let that process unfold naturally" and allow them to "be the person they are." Moreover, "clamping down on your child" often causes them to rebel and can "sabotage the whole effort," she said. The veteran admissions advisor said that hiring a counselor is a superior option. They have "all sorts of resources, insights, understandings about both the process, and eventually the child, that will make everybody more content, that will make the process smoother and more successful," she said. They can give tailored advice to parents about opportunities that suit their child's personality, keep them interested and learning, and set them apart from other candidates when they apply to college, Blackman said. In cases where a child is being prepared to steward the family fortune one day, a counselor can help them develop the traits and skills they'll need to take on that responsibility, she said. For example, they might help them find the right mentors and role models to learn what they need to know. She added that counselors guide not only the child through a process of self-discovery, as they figure out who they are and what's important to them, but they also help parents to understand their role in the process. Blackman said the "most successful parents, with the most successful children, are the ones that have allowed their children to follow their heart ." Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: What RTO personality type are you?
items.summary: As RTO mandates have solidified, employees have developed routines for their in-office days. Nick Lachance/Toronto Star via Getty Images We spoke to half a dozen workers about their RTO routines — whether they love or loathe the office. One manager said he likes to go in every day and that anything else creates confusion. What kind of RTO-er are you? A 5-day faithful, an office recluse, or a remote-work convert? Let us know. Every office has them. The employee who treats work like a second home. The one who arrives before sunrise and disappears by lunch. The midweek warrior. The stealth drop-in. As the return-to-office wars have subsided , they've left behind a workplace ecosystem populated by distinct species whose routines are shaped by a mix of company policy and personal preference. Business Insider spoke with a half-dozen office workers about how they navigate workplace expectations around office attendance — and why they've landed on the routines they have: The 5-day faithful Shaohua Zhou is unapologetically pro-office. The engineering manager, based in San Francisco, spent years working remotely until he joined an agentic software development startup about a year ago. The company's guidance was to come into the office as often as possible. Zhou interpreted that as five days a week. While many coworkers came in three days a week and worked from home in the mornings, Zhou was in the office from 9 a.m. to 6 p.m. every weekday. The schedule made picking up his kids more difficult, but as a manager overseeing 15 people, he wanted to make sure no one came into the office expecting to find him and discovered he wasn't there. "You want to set the example that you value the office," Zhou said. For Zhou, though, it wasn't just about optics. He said working from his living room left him feeling "very trapped," while the office offered more space, better coffee and food, and even a commute he enjoyed. The 30- to 40-minute drive helped him "quiet" his mind and think through priorities before the workday. "For managers, there's a lot of planning that you have in your mind," Zhou said. "You think about, 'Should I focus on this project? Should I focus on these people?'" Zhou left his last company about two months ago for an AI lab where he works over 60 hours a week. Even so, he said he believes anything short of a five-day office expectation creates confusion, with some employees showing up twice a week while managers feel pressure to be there every day. The early bird Before leaving her job in July to start business school, Gricelda Ramos got to try an experiment most office workers never do: choosing her own workday. Her employer offered four eight-hour shifts, with start times ranging from 7 a.m. to 10 a.m. Ramos didn't hesitate. "When I was looking at the time slots and understanding Miami traffic patterns, I really wanted to indulge in the luxury of time," she said. Choosing a 7 a.m. to 3 p.m. schedule cut her morning commute to 15 or 20 minutes. Had she picked a traditional 9-to-5, she said, the drive could have stretched to 45 minutes or an hour. "It was a very minor change," Ramos said. "But it made a huge impact on my quality of life." Ramos said she's learned that flexibility matters more than any single schedule. "I don't think we're all the same kind of worker," Ramos said. The midweek warrior Ian Antonoff's team plans to go in on Tuesdays and Thursdays. He opts to go in on Wednesdays, too. The PR staffer works from a shared coworking space in New York's Flatiron district Tuesday through Thursday, building his day around the commute to Manhattan. He starts with a workout class at Barry's, SoulCycle, or Y7, then settles in from 9 a.m. to 6 p.m. "I think there's so much good that comes in a PR world from collaborating and being able to bounce ideas off of people," Antonoff said. He said his team often grabs lunch together, where conversations drift from client work to the latest season of "Euphoria." "You just turn to the left or fold your laptop down and talk to the person across from you," Antonoff said. "Versus Slack, or 'Hey, can you jump on a huddle?'" While he said he enjoys separating the space between where he lives and where he works, three days is still his sweet spot. Antonoff, who lives in Long Island City, values the flexibility of working remotely on Mondays and Fridays. That lets him go on runs after work with his local run club on Fridays, work from coffee shops, and visit his family and in-laws in the summer. The office tourist Stephen Napolitano's employer asks workers to come into the office between two and eight days a month. The accountant, based in Massachusetts, keeps it simple: every other Wednesday, when the rest of his team comes in. The schedule is predictable enough that he doesn't have to waste time worrying about it. The in-office days are reserved for meetings, catching up with colleagues, and anything that's easier to do face-to-face. Napolitano arrives around 7 a.m. and leaves by 4 p.m. to beat traffic. Leaving an hour later, he said, can double his commute. Beyond that, there's little reason for him to come in more often. The office has a cubicle and a break room, though it doesn't offer much else in the realm of perks, Napolitano said. The office recluse Then there are the employees who come into the office — yet spend their days cooped up behind a closed door. Paul Crockett's company recently introduced a soft return-to-office mandate. Crockett, based in Cary, North Carolina, started by coming in two days a week and has now increased it to three days a week, as requested by the firm. If it were up to him, he'd stick with two days. Even though he comes in regularly, the software developer spends most office days working alone in a private room, even as the workplace around him is mostly full. Most of the seven or eight people on his team work remotely, so he rarely collaborates in person. While one or two might occasionally come in, he's never bumped into them. Despite this, Crockett says he still likes coming in. "It makes me, I think, feel a little more connected with the work and the company." The remote-work convert Before the pandemic, Devin Boudreaux liked a clean line between his work as a PR strategist and his Boise, Idaho, home. At the office, he had a slick setup with multiple monitors and a desk that could be raised and lowered. That wasn't the case at home, and he didn't want those worlds to overlap. Then, as he and his colleagues settled into their lockdown routines, his employer gave them permission to take their monitors and keyboards home. After that, he said, no one wanted to go back. Six years later, the 39-year-old isn't eager to return to an office. While he sometimes misses the spontaneous conversations and says it's harder to build relationships over Slack, the tradeoff is worth it. When Boudreaux was in an office, he would often use his lunch break to race home to check on his dog, who had an autoimmune disorder, and then hurry back and end up eating at his desk. Now, as a full-time remote worker, when something in the older home Boudreaux rents with his girlfriend needs fixing, he doesn't worry about being available for an appointment window spanning several hours. Or, when inspiration strikes at 11 p.m. on a Friday, Boudreaux can simply open his work laptop. Because he gets results, he's not worried about being present for his employer. "If you do good work, then people really aren't going to second-guess," he said. What kind of RTO-er are you? Let us know below: Read the original article on Business Insider
