items.title: Nissan's in-factory AI cameras track how factory workers bend, walk, and build cars
items.summary: Nissan adopted AI to save time on the assembly line — then discovered its biggest benefit was worker safety. Nissan Nissan is using AI-powered cameras at its Canton, Mississippi, plant. They analyze how workers bend, walk, and assemble vehicles The company says the system has contributed to about $34 million in health and safety-related savings. In Canton, Mississippi, where Nissan assembles the Altima sedan and the Frontier pickup, there are cameras watching how workers move. The automaker says the AI-powered system is saving it millions of dollars — and ensuring that factory workers stay healthy. "We're not talking about job elimination," Victor Taylor, Nissan's divisional vice president of manufacturing for the Americas, told Business Insider. "What we're referring to are mundane tasks that are really antiquated for a human being to be performing." Nissan is the latest in a string of automobile companies highlighting how AI is changing the way Americans build cars, including improvements in initial quality and shorter development times . But it is among the few willing to talk openly about how AI is watching its workers. AI that fixes how workers bend and twist A Nissan employee puts a window trim on an Altima sedan. Nissan Chi Amaechi, a Nissan process engineer and former safety engineer who worked on the system's implementation, said the Canton assembly plant has what it calls a "golden cycle" for each job. The golden cycle represents the standard way a task should be performed, including the sequence for installing vehicle components, the time it should take, and body movements designed to reduce repetitive strain. "What it does is it monitors body angles proactively," she said while showing Business Insider a virtual demonstration. "It's basically identifying your joints, so it can identify when a person is bending in a position that's beyond the safety requirement." The system can detect when an employee bends too far or holds an unsafe position for too long, then flag the potential risk for factory managers. Supervisors and engineers can use that information to coach workers, reallocate tasks, or redesign a workstation. Amaechi said the technology replaces time-consuming manual observations that can be inconsistent because employees may change their behavior when they know someone is watching. According to Taylor, Nissan initially evaluated the technology to improve manufacturing efficiency and help train new workers. The ergonomic benefits emerged later. "We weren't originally looking for that," he said of the safety applications. "It just kind of shown itself as, this is the biggest win." The technology has also become part of Nissan's response to an aging workforce, Taylor said. "We have employees that have been in the plant 20, 30-some odd years, and they want to retire," he added. "You can't replace 20, 30 years of know-how." Taylor said employees were involved early through plant safety committees. He and Amaechi said workers initially worried that the technology could threaten jobs, but became more receptive when Nissan presented it as a safety and training tool. They also described instances in which workers welcomed changes made using the system. Overall, Taylor said the technology has contributed to about $34 million in safety and health-related savings at Canton. The system is deployed only in Canton. Taylor said Nissan plans to complete its rollout there before expanding it to the company's Smyrna, Tennessee, assembly plant and evaluating applications at its powertrain facilities. A big turnaround Nissan calls itself America's "fastest-growing mainstream brand" in the auto industry. Marcin Golba/NurPhoto via Getty Images Nissan has had a rough few years, but it is showing early signs of a turnaround. The automaker replaced Makoto Uchida with Ivan Espinosa as CEO in April 2025, shortly after Nissan and Honda abandoned merger talks . Espinosa subsequently introduced a recovery plan centered on cutting jobs , reducing manufacturing capacity, and streamlining Nissan's operations. Canton's assembly line has been affected by some of those cuts: In May, the company canceled its $500 million plan to manufacture electric vehicles at the plant. On Monday, Nissan reported its first quarterly net profit in two years, helped by cost reductions and stronger sales in the US and Japan. The automaker said its US sales rose nearly 10% during the quarter and called itself the fastest-growing mainstream brand over the previous 10 months. But it is among the few willing to talk openly about how AI is watching its workers.

AI that fixes how workers bend and twistA Nissan employee puts a window trim on an Altima sedan.

Nissan

Chi Amaechi, a Nissan process engineer and former safety engineer who worked on the system's implementation, said the Canton assembly plant has what it calls a "golden cycle" for each job.

The golden cycle represents the standard way a task should be performed, including the sequence for installing vehicle components, the time it should take, and body movements designed to reduce repetitive strain.

"What it does is it monitors body angles proactively," she said while showing Business Insider a virtual demonstration. "It's basically identifying your joints, so it can identify when a person is bending in a position that's beyond the safety requirement."

The system can detect when an employee bends too far or holds an unsafe position for too long, then flag the potential risk for factory managers. Supervisors and engineers can use that information to coach workers, reallocate tasks, or redesign a workstation.

Amaechi said the technology replaces time-consuming manual observations that can be inconsistent because employees may change their behavior when they know someone is watching.

According to Taylor, Nissan initially evaluated the technology to improve manufacturing efficiency and help train new workers. The ergonomic benefits emerged later.

"We weren't originally looking for that," he said of the safety applications. "It just kind of shown itself as, this is the biggest win."

The technology has also become part of Nissan's response to an aging workforce, Taylor said.

"We have employees that have been in the plant 20, 30-some odd years, and they want to retire," he added. "You can't replace 20, 30 years of know-how."

Taylor said employees were involved early through plant safety committees. He and Amaechi said workers initially worried that the technology could threaten jobs, but became more receptive when Nissan presented it as a safety and training tool. They also described instances in which workers welcomed changes made using the system.

Overall, Taylor said the technology has contributed to about $34 million in safety and health-related savings at Canton.

The system is deployed only in Canton. Taylor said Nissan plans to complete its rollout there before expanding it to the company's Smyrna, Tennessee, assembly plant and evaluating applications at its powertrain facilities.

A big turnaroundNissan calls itself America's "fastest-growing mainstream brand" in the auto industry.

Marcin Golba/NurPhoto via Getty Images

Nissan has had a rough few years, but it is showing early signs of a turnaround.

The automaker replaced Makoto Uchida with Ivan Espinosa as CEO in April 2025, shortly after Nissan and Honda abandoned merger talks. Espinosa subsequently introduced a recovery plan centered on cutting jobs, reducing manufacturing capacity, and streamlining Nissan's operations.

Canton's assembly line has been affected by some of those cuts: In May, the company canceled its $500 million plan to manufacture electric vehicles at the plant.

On Monday, Nissan reported its first quarterly net profit in two years, helped by cost reductions and stronger sales in the US and Japan. The automaker said its US sales rose nearly 10% during the quarter and called itself the fastest-growing mainstream brand over the previous 10 months.

The company calls itself America's "fastest-growing mainstream" car brand, per sales.

items.title: Ikea is growing its resale business. It's attracting bargain hunters and design nerds.
items.summary: Next month, Ikea will expand its buyback and resell program to all US stores. Ikea Ikea has bought back about 53,000 items through its secondhand division over the past five years. The Swedish retailer is expanding the buyback program to all US stores in September. The program appeals to price-savvy shoppers as well as design lovers , Ikea told Business Insider. Your old Ikea bookshelf is part of a growing secondhand market. Ikea has spent five years growing its buyback and resell division, which pays customers for their old Ikea-brand furniture in store credit and resells it at the chain's stores. In September, buyback and resell will be available in every full-format US Ikea store when the retailer starts offering the option at its Brooklyn store, said Bryan Walker, country product quality manager for Ikea US. For shoppers, buying secondhand has long been a way to save money across a range of products. It's also become a bigger business over the last several years, from side-hustlers selling clothes on marketplaces like Depop to major brands like REI selling used outdoor gear. Used furniture has a particular attraction because of the high price of buying new pieces, and customers can often find designs not readily seen in large showrooms. Nowadays, sites like Facebook Marketplace and Craigslist are packed with used furniture from all eras. At Ikea, the buyback program has taken back about 53,000 items over the past five years, Walker said. Customers get a quote showing how much Ikea will pay them for their furniture on Ikea's website. Then, they can bring it into a store to drop it off and get their credit. For a large black Kallax bookcase with minor scratches, for example, Ikea will pay $69.65 at a store in the Washington, DC area, according to the website . An "as new" version would be worth about $10 more, while a "well-used" bookcase would earn about $10 less. A new version of the bookcase sells for almost $300. Ikea employees inspect the items that the company buys back. In some cases, the furniture needs cleaning or repair before the company puts it up for sale at in the As-Is section, Walker said. From cheap bookcases to post-modern desks Many of the items that the stores repurchase are used — and therefore cheaper — versions of what it sells new in the stores. That appeals to customers who are trying to save money, Walker said. "I can't have a conversation about secondhand without talking about affordability," he told Business Insider. Other items attract more design-focused shoppers. Walker said that some Ikea stores have bought back pieces from its Stockholm collection, a higher-priced line that includes a sofa that costs $2,000 new. A couple of months ago, one Ikea store bought back the program's oldest piece of furniture to date: A post-modern Signatur executive desk that Ikea started selling in the 1980s — the same decade it opened its first US stores. Pieces like the desk appeal to customers who are looking for a specific style, Walker said. "It's just the perfect encapsulation of really simple form," he said. Customers who participate in the buyback program visit an Ikea store 50% more on average in the six months afterward, Walker said — "a really significant impact" that creates more loyal customers, he said. "A lot of businesses see secondhand as a side business," Walker said. "I do see this as a growth area for us." Do you have a story idea about Ikea? items.title: KKR shared profits from a big sale with employees. Here's what they're doing with the windfall.
items.summary: Bonnie Stewart, a longtime ISC employee, shortly after finding out about her payout. KKR Workers at ISC got a big payout when KKR sold the company, with one worker receiving $413,000. The payouts are part of a broader KKR initiative to spread employee ownership across private equity. We spoke to three workers about the experience and how they were spending their windfall. In his 12 years on the job, Justin Berk, a 44-year-old product manager at an insurance-tech company, had seen his employer get bought and sold twice. All he had received in return was a "pat on the back" at a company meeting. "A pat on the back is nice, but it doesn't pay the bills," he said. When KKR sold his company, Integrated Specialty Coverages, to Onex Partners, the company meeting was much more significant: Berk received 30 months of his salary as a cash bonus as part of a KKR initiative to share its private equity profits with workers at its portfolio companies. Berk and other long-tenured employees, like Bonnie Stewart, the director of operations for ISC subsidiary Gaslamp Insurance Services, received 30 months of their salaries. The payouts were announced at a September 18 meeting in San Diego's iconic Hotel Del Coronado, following a Champagne toast in celebration of the sale, in which KKR said it delivered a 2.5 return. Stewart said that if she could "bottle up the feeling" of receiving that windfall, she "wouldn't sell it." The change in mindset that came with the program, starting at the foundational level of renaming "employees" as "owners," and the hard work that led to the profitable sale, were worth even more. "I don't think Travis Kelce would sell the feeling of winning a Super Bowl," Stewart said. "He earned that. His team earned that." ISC employees celebrate their payout at the Hotel Del Coronado. KKR In total, KKR paid nearly 400 ISC employees between 3 and 30 months of their salary after closing the sale. Payouts were based on when workers joined the company, and ranged from a minimum of $10,000 to a maximum payout of more than $413,000. The average payout for workers who joined in 2025 was $24,500. It is part of a KKR initiative that's helped profit-sharing gain steam across the industry . KKR has exited 15 of the 91 companies it has programs with, delivering $2 billion to more than 40,000 employees. These employees don't receive actual shares when KKR buys a company; instead, a portion of the company's equity is earmarked for them. Their potential payout, just like KKR's, is based on the return it gets on that initial investment. We spoke to three ISC employees, who told us that the money was life-changing, allowing two to save up for a down payment in a pricey Southern California housing market. Justin Berk and his wife went on vacation in Laguna Beach shortly after his big payday. Justin Berk Berk took his two daughters, 12 and 10, to Maui, Hawaii, for the first time last year, a vacation that wasn't possible before. He's also no longer wincing at fees for club sports. "It's easier now to say yes to more meaningful family choices," Berk said. The cash Payouts were made when the deal closed on November 24 of last year, and were based on the employee's current salary and tenure at the company. Stewart, who started at the company 19 years ago, was among the employees who received the highest monthly payout. She has two younger kids and said the money is "very impactful" on her family, allowing her to think about creating wealth for her children . It's expensive to live in Southern California, and it can be hard to save. "It gave us that new opportunity to look at investments that we might not necessarily know of before," Stewart said. KKR provided free financial advisors to employee owners as part of the deal. Stewart and her colleagues even asked executives how they managed their money to learn how to handle their coming windfall. Year they joined ISC Payout 2025 Greater of 3 months or $10,000 2024 Greater of 6 months or $25,000 2023 Greater of 9 months or $35,000 2022 Greater of 12 months or $45,000 Sept 2015 - 2021 Greater of 15 months or $70,000 Before September 2015 (More than 10 years of tenure) Greater of 30 months or $115,000 Trevor Sybert, a 49-year-old underwriter who joined the company in 2020, had scheduled a work trip to South Carolina, so he watched the meeting over Zoom in an airport alongside another executive. He was "bummed" to miss the event live, but most importantly, he was going to get 15 months' pay. Right now, he said, the money is sitting in a high-yield savings account, but he plans to use it as a down payment on a condo, as he and his wife divorced and sold their house. Trevor Sybert is saving up for a down payment on a condo. Trevor Sybert He's feeling real "financial freedom," he said, and plans to be conservative with his spending. Sybert said his financial advisor also helped him set up his financial future following his divorce. The first step was growing the size of his emergency fund. For Berk, the money means that he can do more things with his family. But most importantly, it means that his family can have a home of their own. "Saving up for a down payment out here is almost impossible unless you're an executive at a company," Berk said. "Now, I have a nice cushion that will become a down payment on a house." The change When KKR bought the company in 2021, Sybert instantly saw the appeal of the ownership program: "We are going to make some money if the business does well," he said. Sybert said he learned more about business than ever before — "This is the first time I've ever heard of EBITDA," he said — attending quarterly owners' meetings that got deep into the details on ISC's performance. KKR has built and iterated on an in-house playbook for these investments, which it has now helped export to other industry leaders, such as Apollo, through the nonprofit Ownership Works. Blackstone, which is not part of the initiative but has made its own employee-ownership pledge, recently took a company with an employee-ownership plan, Jersey Mike's, public for the first time . At the beginning, the workers, redubbed " owners" as part of KKR's initiative, were given a crash course in valuation, the company's business plan, and how it gets its revenue. Each quarter, company leaders would walk through the company's projected valuation and give a performance scorecard. Information became increasingly transparent throughout the process, said Berk, with many employees gaining direct access to business intelligence dashboards to understand the gritty details of the business. But it's the behavior that information fostered that really made the difference. "When you own a piece of it, you're not just clocking out and saying, 'Well, I'm done for the day,'" Berk said. "You might stick around a little later, do a little extra, make that extra trip to the broker. You're owed a little piece of the pie, so you're going to take better care of it." It also meant that employees who weren't willing to adopt the mindset left over time, Berk said, while the rest stayed. He said his team had only lost one member in three years. The company created the Bright Ideas club, a place for workers to pitch potential big-picture changes at the company, as well as a Founders Club, which highlighted the top five employee-owners each year. ISC employees celebrate their payouts at the iconic Hotel Del Coronado. ISC For Stewart, who had started as a receptionist before rising to her current role managing roughly 20 employees, the switch from employer to "owner" was natural. She said she noticed a change in how her team would come in with new ideas to solve problems. Her fellow owners were "thinking outside of the box," she said. "In retrospect, we grew a lot, and for the best," she said. Over the years, it also became apparent that the company was edging closer to a sale, with metrics improving at each quarterly meeting. Stewart found out about an event invite two days before the event. All signs pointed to good news, but "I did not want to say it out loud," Stewart said. But as she saw balloons lining the entrance way and cameras and light set-ups, she could sigh a deep breath. Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: A woman built her parents a 725-square-foot cottage in her backyard so they could be closer to their grandchildren
items.summary: Caitlin Swann and her kids see her parents daily. The Picket Fence Projects Caitlin Swann lives in Connecticut with her family. In 2024, she and her husband built a small cottage for her parents on her property. Now, Patti and Gary Christie live steps away from their grandchildren. Caitlin Swann doesn't have to look far when she needs a babysitter. In fact, she can just walk into her backyard and knock on her parents' door. Swann's parents live in an accessory dwelling unit, or ADU, on her Connecticut property. Their one-bedroom, one-bathroom cottage is mere steps away from Swann's home. They see their daughter and her three children daily since they moved in. "It's the best," Swann told Business Insider of their multigenerational home . "I pinch myself." In 2024, Patti and Gary Christie were trying to decide where to live. The Picket Fence Projects Patti and Gary Christie were at a crossroads in 2024. The 74- and 75-year-olds had lived in their family home for over 40 years, raising their children there. After retiring and becoming grandparents, they were ready to sell their home, but they weren't sure where to go next. Their three children are spread out across the tri-state area. They liked Fairfield, Connecticut, where their daughter Caitlin Swann, 42, lived, but the houses they could afford there didn't thrill them. "We looked at houses, but what they would get for what they would have to pay was a little depressing," Swann said. Then, Swann had an idea. The Picket Fence Projects Swann had moved into her Fairfield home with her husband and three kids in 2023. Swann is an interior designer, and she has worked painstakingly since they moved in to make the three-bedroom, two-and-a-half-bathroom house feel like theirs. (It will soon have four bedrooms and three and a half baths when they wrap their current renovation.) As Swann was chatting with her parents about what to do about their house, an ad for a "granny pod" popped up on her Facebook in November 2024. " Granny pods " are pre-fab ADUs that people can add to their properties, specifically designed with aging parents in mind. "I had thought, 'Oh, we could probably add on to the house,' but I didn't really think about a separate structure," Swann said. Swann sent her mom a screenshot of the ad in jest, but to her surprise, her mom took the idea seriously. "She was like, 'That's brilliant,'" Swann said. They decided to build a custom ADU for the Christies on Swann's property. The Picket Fence Projects After seeing the ad, Swann looked into local zoning laws about building an ADU in her area, unsure if it was even possible to add a new structure to their half-acre property. To her delight, it was. Swann, her husband, and her parents chatted it over and decided that building the ADU, which they call their tiny cottage, was the right move for everyone. The Swanns both have close relationships with her parents, and Swann said her parents' lifestyle felt well-suited to living on the same property. "My parents are really respectful," she said. "They're not overbearing. They're extremely helpful. They go to bed really early." "I guess you don't really know until it happens, but I know I had no concerns about living on the same property," she added. The Christies financed the build, and Swann assembled a team to bring it to life. The Picket Fence Projects Because the ADU would be their home, the Christies paid for the build , not the Swanns. "We did not spend a dime of our own personal money," Swann said. The Christies lived in their home in New Jersey for most of the build, and they then stayed with Swann's uncle for the last stretch. Swann took the lead on designing the 725-square-foot space, both because of her experience with interior design and her parents' disinterest in that part of the process. "My mom was like, 'I don't want to make any decisions,'" Swann said. "But of course, I ran a lot of ideas past her to make sure that she liked what I was doing." Swann collaborated with Eileen Duffy, an architect with whom she frequently works, and tapped Paul Delco Builders as her contractor. They broke ground in May 2025, and the project was completed in November of the same year. Swann designed the ADU to blend well with the main house. The Picket Fence Projects Because the main house and the ADU would be so close together, Swann wanted them to feel like they went together. "I wanted it to feel really cohesive with our house, especially from the exterior," Swann said. For instance, Swann based the cottage's exterior design on her house, essentially making the ADU look like a smaller version of it. They have the same roof, copper gutters, and even the same siding. The exterior also features two Dutch doors for indoor-outdoor living and a brick fireplace. The covered porch is one of the Christies' favorite parts of their home. The Picket Fence Projects Swann said she knew a covered porch was a must for her parents' home, as they had one at their old home and loved it. items.title: Dietitians agree — cut back on 1 thing for better gut health, energy, and lower risk of cancer
items.summary: Swapping out sugary drinks for plain water or seltzer has major benefits for your health. parichat wongyai/Getty Images Sugary drinks may be one of the worst kinds of ultra-processed foods for your health, dietitians say. Too much sugar in soda or energy drinks is linked to risks like cancer, heart disease, and diabetes. Diet sodas may be a helpful alternative, but aren't risk-free, and can mess with gut health. Diet advice is rarely one-size-fits-all. But one particular vice — enjoyed daily by more than half of Americans — has become the bane of health experts. Dietitians really, really want us to step away from the sugary soda . At a recent nutrition conference in Washington, DC, with more than 3,000 professionals, I asked around about what we should all be eating more of. While everyone had a different answer, nearly all agreed on what to avoid: cutting back on sugary drinks is a simple way to improve your health. The dietitians (and doctors and researchers) I spoke with had a long list of reasons you should consider swapping out soda, from blood sugar crashes to potential links to increased cancer risk. Here's what we know about why soda may be uniquely harmful, and you may be better off eating ice cream instead. Why is soda bad for you? The problem with soda and other sweet drinks is that they're a major source of added sugar, often in huge amounts. The recommended daily limit for added sugar ranges from 25 grams to 50 grams, per the American Heart Association and the USDA, while a typical can of soda contains about 40 grams of sugar. Too much sugar is linked to a wide array of health issues, such as: Type 2 diabetes Cancer (including colon cancer , now the leading cause of cancer-related death in people under 50) Obesity and related health issues, including metabolic syndrome Heart disease Tooth decay Liver damage Kidney disease Sweetened drinks are a particularly concentrated source of sugar, which means the side effects can hit harder: for instance, causing more intense blood sugar spikes and crashes. Marian Neuhouser, one of the dietitians who told me we should cut back, studies diet and cancer risk at the Fred Hutchinson Cancer Center in Seattle. Some of her work has found that drinking more sugar is linked to a higher risk of cancer. And sugary drinks are more closely linked to cancer risk than almost any other ultra-processed food (except processed red meat like bacon), said Kenny Mendoza, a professor at the University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center. "Definitely, I would recommend avoiding ultra-processed sugary drinks and ultra-processed meats because those are actually consistently associated with a higher risk of cancer," Mendoza said. Sodas are the most popular sweet drink, but the advice also applies to other beverages with added sugar, including energy drinks, fruit drinks (except for 100% juice), sports drinks (yes, even with electrolytes), and sweetened coffee or tea. Other ultra-processed foods can be high in sugar, too, from obvious sweet treats like pastries and cookies to sneaky sources of sugar like bread, condiments, and yogurt. Sugary beverages may be especially harmful, however, because they add calories and sugar without providing much nutritional value, and the liquid form makes it easy to consume too much. Nicholas Marchello, a registered dietitian and nutrition professor at the University of Central Missouri, said he'd rather see people eat ice cream than drink soda. "There are no benefits. It's just sugar; it's going to leave your stomach in seconds. At least ice cream would fill you up," he said. Is diet soda healthier? If you're a regular soda sipper, your first instinct may be to switch to sugar-free, but it can have mixed benefits, according to the latest research. Reducing your overall sugar intake is a good thing, so diet soda can be a smart way to cut back. However, it may not be completely risk-free. Emerging evidence suggests that alternative sweeteners may have side effects of their own. Popular sweeteners like aspartame, sucralose , and stevia have been linked to disruptions in the gut microbiome. Over the long term, too much of these compounds may be linked to risks for heart health or metabolism, a recent study suggests. The strongest evidence on potential issues linked to artificial sweeteners comes from studies on mice and rats, often given doses many times higher than what any human would drink. Rigorous long-term studies on specific ingredients and human health are notoriously difficult to do. There have been observational studies in humans that have found a link between higher intake of artificial sweeteners and increased risk of heart attack , as well as metabolic changes . These studies show a correlation, but don't prove that the artificial sweeteners cause these health issues, so further research is needed to better understand how they might affect our long-term health. For now, the best advice from doctors and dietitians is to drink mostly plain water throughout the day. For a bit of fizz and flavor, opt for seltzer or 100% fruit juice. If you need an energy boost, lean into coffee and tea, which have extra health benefits as long as you skip the cream and sugar. Read the original article on Business Insider

items.summary: VistaJet This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Thomas Flohr, the 65-year-old founder, chairman, and CEO of VistaJet, based in St. Moritz, Switzerland, about his daily routine. It's been edited for length and clarity. I started my career at a Chicago-based technology firm in 1985 and rose through the ranks. I later acquired most of the company's European operations through my company, Comprendium Investment. My frequent business travel in the early 2000s exposed me to the shortcomings of private aviation. At the time, I found the private jet experience to be inconsistent and underwhelming. The service quality didn't match the level of luxury that clients paying $10,000 to $15,000 an hour expected. I didn't see a good solution in the market and initially thought about paying for fractional jet ownership before deciding against it. Business Insider's Power Hours series gives readers an inside look at how powerful leaders in business structure their workday. Reach out to editor Lauryn Haas to share your daily routine. After exploring all other options, I bought a Learjet 60 in 2003, and that plane became the foundation for starting VistaJet in 2004. Vista is a private aviation subscription service that provides access to over 270 customized business jets for clients in 187 countries. My primary job is building client relationships and setting the company's strategic direction. items.title: I build AI data centers. I want them to disappear from view.
items.summary: Sean James works at Nvidia as a distinguished engineer. Sean James Sean James is a distinguished engineer at AI chipmaker Nvidia focused on powering data centers. James started his career as a submarine electrician in the Navy and previously spent 25 years building data centers at Microsoft. He makes the case that AI data centers "need to fade into the background" so they're visibly "unremarkable." This first-person essay was written by Sean James , a distinguished engineer in energy systems at Nvidia, where he works on the power and energy infrastructure needed to support AI data centers. He previously spent more than two decades at Microsoft designing and building data centers. Chances are you passed an electrical substation today that delivers power to thousands of homes at hundreds of thousands of volts. It was so unremarkable that you didn't even notice. Sometime in the past, these marvels of engineering simply vanished into the background. For most of my career, when asked, I told people I built data centers . And only in the last five years did people know what one even was. I still don't think my mom knows what I do. Contrast that with today and how often I get calls and see texts asking this and that about data centers. Mostly, it's questions about water usage and energy demand . Data centers went from large concrete buildings assumed to be just another warehouse to headline news. And I want them to disappear again. I recently left Microsoft where I spent 25 years operating, designing, building, and toward the end, innovation. Innovation was all about making data centers less resource intensive, faster to build, and modular so they would come together like Lego bricks. Last month, while cleaning out my home office, I came across a page of notes from 2015. Scrawled across the top: Top 3 Career Goals. One of them read: disappear the data center. This remains the goal. "The most profound technologies are those that disappear." - Mark, Weiser, Scientific American, September 1991. Disappearing tech can still be seen; I am not talking about hiding it. Technology matures until it blends into daily life and stops asking for attention. It becomes unremarkable. Like water mains and substations, infrastructure graduates when it stops being news, stops demanding attention from us. Two decades ago, our focus was to keep data centers invisible by making sure they were always online and powered up and never the source of an outage. Sean James previously spent 25 years designing and building data centers for Microsoft. Sean James Now think of a data center like a factory. An industrial engineer's job is to identify and kill all non-value-added parts. A slug of steel goes in one end, and a wheel comes out the other end, and the mission is to make everything in the middle as elegant, fast, and efficient as possible. The AI factory works the same way, turning electricity into tokens. Unfortunately, data centers are not disappearing today. I would not want to live next to one. Loud, dust, traffic, water, interactions with the grid. The North American Electric Reliability Corporation (NERC) issued a rare Level 3 alert in May, its highest tier. The trigger: events where more than 1,000 megawatts of data center load dropped off the grid in seconds. Voltage dips are common on the grid, and we don't even notice them in our homes. But data centers are designed to protect their servers. When they sense a dip, they let go of the grid and jump to onsite batteries. The computers ride through without a blink. The grid takes the hit. This type of disappearing makes our grid unstable. Believe me or don't, but I have watched the data center diminish over the decades. Energy needed to cool servers dropped when evaporative cooling replaced chillers. Server companies keep relaxing temperature requirements to make servers easier to cool. PUE, the measure of how energy efficient a data center is, has gone from 3 to 5 in the 90s to 1.2 to 1.5 today. Waste, too. I remember mountains of foam from server packaging. Now racks arrive fully assembled in reusable wooden boxes. Safety at data center projects has become the highest priority. Workers go home whole and projects are uneventful. And those of us who design them are still not satisfied. Chasing the next breakthrough is what gets us out of bed in the morning. Today, the data center is starting to vanish one piece at a time. Nvidia , where I work now, went public this summer with a design that runs coolant at up to 113 degrees, hotter than a hot tub. At that temperature, heat exchangers and outside air can carry the heat away in most climates. No cooling towers. Cooling water use at the site drops to zero. Data centers are also learning to be grid assets instead of liabilities. Grid stabilizers. Flexing to hand capacity back when the grid is stressed. Riding through voltage dips instead of letting go. Even the diesel generators are starting to disappear from the design, replaced by fault-tolerant networks, batteries, and fuel cells. The criticism of data centers is important feedback. A lot of it is accurate. Some of it is not. The encouraging part for me is to see the open dialog. Data center designers can't improve in a vacuum. And the local jurisdictions that set the rules for construction need to modernize them, so that development of any kind meets the needs of the communities that host it. Substations and water towers are critical to modern life. They surround us, quietly hidden in plain sight. Data centers need to fade into the background too, and that is the goal of every data center designer. We will continue to make them efficient, sustainable, and eventually unremarkable. Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: Why billion-dollar robotics startups are obsessed with folding laundry
items.summary: Weave Robotics' Isaac 1 robot. Weave Robotics Billion-dollar robotics startups are racing to teach robots to fold laundry. Laundry is a safe, contained test for robots entering the chaos of the home, roboticists say. Home robots must learn more chores to justify their steep prices. Before Silicon Valley's robots take over, they have to learn to fold your underwear. In recent months, some of the buzziest robotics startups — including Figure AI , Sunday Robotics, and Weave Robotics — have shown off robots that autonomously fold clothes. Together, the companies have raised billions of dollars at lofty valuations, as investors bet that home robots are finally nearing a commercial breakthrough. We were promised robot butlers. For now, Silicon Valley would like to help you match your socks. Home robotics companies are focusing on laundry because it's an ideal first task. It is difficult enough to showcase a machine's intelligence and physical control, and safe enough that failure carries few consequences, roboticists say. It is also a chore almost everyone does, and few enjoy. Consumers don't need to know how AI works to appreciate a robot that turns a crumpled pile of clothes into a neat stack. Teaching a robot to fold clothing has long been a "holy grail" of the field, said roboticist and Spelman College president Ayanna Howard. That's because robots must learn to handle "deformable objects" — clothes that bunch, fold, and wrinkle — and manipulate them with enough precision to fold them well. Weave Robotics' Isaac 1 robot. Weave Robotics "This is one of the most challenging dexterous manipulation tasks for a humanoid robot," Figure wrote in a blog post last year. Sunday CEO Tony Zhao told Business Insider that the company chose laundry partly because it "looks for hard things to do." Yet when a robot fails, the stakes are low. "If you drop a piece of clothing, it's not going to break," Howard said. The robotics industry has been through laundry hype cycles before. The Japanese company behind the $16,000 laundry-folding robot, Laundroid, filed for bankruptcy in 2019, and FoldiMate made repeated splashes at the Consumer Electronics Show in the late 2010s but never shipped a product. High costs and poor reliability undid those earlier efforts. Today's startups say that advances in AI, cheaper hardware, and a flood of talent and capital into physical AI will make this generation different — and capable of doing far more than laundry. "For the longest time, the technology just wasn't there," Weave Robotics CEO Kaan Dogrusoz told Business Insider. "But then, everything changed." Whether that’s true is about to be tested outside the lab. The latest robots are expensive, and their reliability in real homes remains unknown because few have been deployed. While this generation can fold laundry much faster than its predecessors, a single item can still take minutes to fold, and unfamiliar clothing can leave the machines stumped. Sunday plans to place its robot in homes through a beta program this fall. Weave and 1X expect to begin delivering robots to customers later this year. Why laundry is a gateway into the home Robotics companies are starting with laundry because it's a bounded task inside the home, a tough environment for robots to navigate. "The home is the ultimate unstructured environment," said Matei Ciocarlie, a mechanical engineering professor at Columbia University who works on robotics. Most robots operate in controlled environments such as factories and warehouses , where their surroundings and movements can be tightly defined. They are often separated from people for safety. The home, by comparison, is a hellscape for robots. Every room is an obstacle course. Pets dart underfoot, and toddlers crawl across the floor, threatening to send machines into a faceplant. Sunday Robotics' Memo robot. Sunday Robotics When folding laundry, a robot can stay in one corner while a hamper of clothes is brought to it, rather than having to navigate the entire house. Dogrusoz cited this as the reason Weave chose laundry as the first task. "It's an attempt to put bounds on the craziness," Ciocarlie said. What comes after laundry? Teaching a robot to fold laundry is one thing. Convincing people to pay thousands of dollars for it is another. Weave's Isaac, for instance, costs $8,000 upfront, or $449 a month through a subscription. For most households, it would likely be cheaper to outsource the chore to a laundromat or a person. Or, as Howard put it: "That's what kids are for." For these robots to make economic sense, they need to do far more than fold clothes. Sunday's AI system, for instance, is learning chores including vacuuming, organizing toys, fastening zippers, and making coffee. 1X is marketing its humanoid robot NEO as a personal housekeeper capable of folding laundry, organizing shelves, and tidying rooms. Weave declined to say which task it is tackling next. 1X's NEO humanoid. Camille Cohen for The Washington Post via Getty Images Howard said consumers are unlikely to seriously consider buying a home robot until it can perform enough useful tasks to justify its price, like heating dinner before its owner gets home, mowing the lawn, or cleaning the pool. The challenge will be building a single robot that can do all of these things. Jason Corso, a robotics professor at the University of Michigan, said companies are "stuck in an appliance mindset," building robots around individual chores rather than machines that can understand context and adapt to people's needs. For many of these companies, getting robots into homes to fold laundry is also the start of what they hope will become an expanding data flywheel. Robotics startups are scrambling for real-world data needed to train the "brains" of their machines. While large language models are trained on internet data, there is no comparable dataset for the physical world. Sunday, for example, trains its AI models on people doing everyday tasks in $200 sensor-equipped gloves that mirror its robots' hands. The most valuable data — the kind that could help companies truly master laundry and expand into other tasks — may come from the robots themselves as they encounter the countless edge cases of real homes. A truly general-purpose home robot — the robot butler Silicon Valley has long promised — is still many years away, Corso said. Have a tip? Contact Rya Jetha via email at rjetha@businessinsider.com or Signal at rjetha.07. Use a personal email address and a nonwork device; here's our guide to sharing information securely. High costs and poor reliability undid those earlier efforts. Today's startups say that advances in AI, cheaper hardware, and a flood of talent and capital into physical AI will make this generation different — and capable of doing far more than laundry.

"For the longest time, the technology just wasn't there," Weave Robotics CEO Kaan Dogrusoz told Business Insider. "But then, everything changed."

Whether that’s true is about to be tested outside the lab. The latest robots are expensive, and their reliability in real homes remains unknown because few have been deployed. While this generation can fold laundry much faster than its predecessors, a single item can still take minutes to fold, and unfamiliar clothing can leave the machines stumped.

Sunday plans to place its robot in homes through a beta program this fall. Weave and 1X expect to begin delivering robots to customers later this year.

Why laundry is a gateway into the home

Robotics companies are starting with laundry because it's a bounded task inside the home, a tough environment for robots to navigate.

"The home is the ultimate unstructured environment," said Matei Ciocarlie, a mechanical engineering professor at Columbia University who works on robotics.

Most robots operate in controlled environments such as factories and warehouses, where their surroundings and movements can be tightly defined. They are often separated from people for safety.

The home, by comparison, is a hellscape for robots. Every room is an obstacle course. Pets dart underfoot, and toddlers crawl across the floor, threatening to send machines into a faceplant.

Sunday Robotics' Memo robot.

Sunday Robotics

When folding laundry, a robot can stay in one corner while a hamper of clothes is brought to it, rather than having to navigate the entire house. Dogrusoz cited this as the reason Weave chose laundry as the first task.

"It's an attempt to put bounds on the craziness," Ciocarlie said.

What comes after laundry?

Teaching a robot to fold laundry is one thing. Convincing people to pay thousands of dollars for it is another.

Weave's Isaac, for instance, costs $8,000 upfront, or $449 a month through a subscription. For most households, it would likely be cheaper to outsource the chore to a laundromat or a person. Or, as Howard put it: "That's what kids are for."

For these robots to make economic sense, they need to do far more than fold clothes.

Sunday's AI system, for instance, is learning chores including vacuuming, organizing toys, fastening zippers, and making coffee. 1X is marketing its humanoid robot NEO as a personal housekeeper capable of folding laundry, organizing shelves, and tidying rooms. Weave declined to say which task it is tackling next.

1X's NEO humanoid.

Camille Cohen for The Washington Post via Getty Images

Howard said consumers are unlikely to seriously consider buying a home robot until it can perform enough useful tasks to justify its price, like heating dinner before its owner gets home, mowing the lawn, or cleaning the pool. The challenge will be building a single robot that can do all of these things.

Jason Corso, a robotics professor at the University of Michigan, said companies are "stuck in an appliance mindset," building robots around individual chores rather than machines that can understand context and adapt to people's needs.

For many of these companies, getting robots into homes to fold laundry is also the start of what they hope will become an expanding data flywheel. Robotics startups are scrambling for real-world data needed to train the "brains" of their machines. While large language models are trained on internet data, there is no comparable dataset for the physical world. Sunday, for example, trains its AI models on people doing everyday tasks in $200 sensor-equipped gloves that mirror its robots' hands.

The most valuable data — the kind that could help companies truly master laundry and expand into other tasks — may come from the robots themselves as they encounter the countless edge cases of real homes.

A truly general-purpose home robot — the robot butler Silicon Valley has long promised — is still many years away, Corso said.

items.title: Google dismantles Deepmind and bets on a fresh start as Hassabis heads for the exit
items.summary: Google Deepmind is losing its autonomy, and founder Demis Hassabis may leave the AI lab for good in the coming months. AI researcher Koray Kavukcuoglu will take over day-to-day operations without the CEO title, and all Gemini development is moving to the Bay Area. Internally, Google is apparently struggling with serious problems training frontier models, even as its cloud business generates billions. The question is whether the company is deliberately betting on infrastructure or simply can't catch the leaders. items.title: AVCaptureMultiCamSession: the real limits, and why the stock Camera app doesn't offer dual recording
items.summary:
Modern iPhones can genuinely run the front and back cameras at the same time. AVCaptureMultiCamSession has been in the SDK since iOS 13 and works on A12 and later hardware. And yet Apple's own Camera app has no dual-recording mode, no toggle, no hidden gesture. That is not a product oversight you can route around. iOS has two separate concepts: a normal AVCaptureSession runs exactly one camera and can switch between them, and a multi-camera session runs several inputs concurrently. The second is a different object with different rules, and almost everything you know about the first one is wrong for it. Here is what those rules actually cost, from a shipping dual-camera recorder. The problem You want one MP4 containing both cameras, composited live, with a preview that matches the file. The pieces sound routine: two inputs, two outputs, a compositor, an AVAssetWriter . Why the obvious approach fails addInput / addOutput simply fail The convenience API implicitly forms connections for you. On a multi-cam session that fails outright. You must add inputs and outputs without connections and wire AVCaptureConnection objects yourself: private func addVideoBranch ( device : AVCaptureDevice , output : AVCaptureVideoDataOutput , mirrored : Bool ) throws { let input = try AVCaptureDeviceInput ( device : device ) guard session . canAddInput ( input ) else { throw ConfigError . cannotAdd ( " \( device . position ) input" ) } session . addInputWithNoConnections ( input ) output . videoSettings = [ kCVPixelBufferPixelFormatTypeKey as String : kCVPixelFormatType_32BGRA ] output . alwaysDiscardsLateVideoFrames = true guard session . canAddOutput ( output ) else { throw ConfigError . cannotAdd ( " \( device . position ) output" ) } session . addOutputWithNoConnections ( output ) guard let port = input . ports ( for : . video , sourceDeviceType : device . deviceType , sourceDevicePosition : device . position ) . first else { throw ConfigError . noPort ( " \( device . position ) " ) } let conn = AVCaptureConnection ( inputPorts : [ port ], output : output ) guard session . canAddConnection ( conn ) else { throw ConfigError . cannotAdd ( " \( device . position ) connection" ) } session . addConnection ( conn ) if conn . isVideoRotationAngleSupported ( 90 ) { conn . videoRotationAngle = 90 } if mirrored , conn . isVideoMirroringSupported { conn . automaticallyAdjustsVideoMirroring = false conn . isVideoMirrored = true } } sessionPreset does not work either A multi-cam session only accepts .inputPriority . Resolution is chosen per device by picking an activeFormat , only from formats where isMultiCamSupported == true — and it must be chosen before addInput : private func configureFormat ( for device : AVCaptureDevice , targetWidth : Int32 ) throws { let multiCamFormats = device . formats . filter { $0 . isMultiCamSupported } guard ! multiCamFormats . isEmpty else { throw ConfigError . noFormat ( " \( device . position ) " ) } func supports30fps ( _ f : AVCaptureDevice . Format ) -> Bool { f . videoSupportedFrameRateRanges . contains { $0 . minFrameRate <= 30 && $0 . maxFrameRate >= 30 } } func dims ( _ f : AVCaptureDevice . Format ) -> CMVideoDimensions { CMVideoFormatDescriptionGetDimensions ( f . formatDescription ) } let chosen = multiCamFormats . first ( where : { dims ( $0 ) . width == targetWidth && supports30fps ( $0 ) }) ?? multiCamFormats . max ( by : { a , b in Int ( dims ( a ) . width ) * Int ( dims ( a ) . height ) < Int ( dims ( b ) . width ) * Int ( dims ( b ) . height ) }) ! try device . lockForConfiguration () defer { device . unlockForConfiguration () } device . activeFormat = chosen let duration = CMTime ( value : 1 , timescale : 30 ) device . activeVideoMinFrameDuration = duration device . activeVideoMaxFrameDuration = duration } Note filter { $0.isMultiCamSupported } . The set of multi-cam formats is a strict subset of what the device offers when it is the only camera running. This is the first place the "why not just do what the Camera app does" answer starts to appear: the Camera app is not choosing from the same menu. The hardwareCost gate — and it cannot be pre-checked This is the constraint that shapes the whole feature. A multi-cam configuration has a hardwareCost and a systemPressureCost . If hardwareCost > 1.0 you get a runtime error and the session dies. And the value only reflects the new configuration after you commit it . There is no dry run. So every configuration change has to be: change → commit → read cost → roll back if over. session . beginConfiguration () do { try configureFormat ( for : back , targetWidth : r . targetWidth ) try configureFormat ( for : front , targetWidth : r . targetWidth ) } catch { session . commitConfiguration () errorMessage = L10n . Error . detail ( Strings . resolutionFailed , error . localizedDescription ) await startSession () return } session . commitConfiguration () if session . hardwareCost > 1.0 { downgraded = true applied = previous session . beginConfiguration () try ? configureFormat ( for : back , targetWidth : previous . targetWidth ) try ? configureFormat ( for : front , targetWidth : previous . targetWidth ) session . commitConfiguration () } Dual 1080p exceeds the budget easily on many devices. That rollback is not defensive tidiness — remove it and you ship an app that dies when a user picks a resolution their phone cannot sustain. The seamless zoom is not available to you The stock Camera app's continuous pinch from ultra-wide through wide to telephoto is built on a virtual capture device that internally owns several physical lenses and crossfades between them. A multi-cam session connects to specific physical devices, because that is what the isMultiCamSupported format check operates on. A virtual device that silently reaches across several lenses is not something that check can reason about. The consequence for the UI is that lens choice and zoom become two different controls, and the lens picker may list fewer lenses than the stock app shows: /// Running three back lenses at once under MultiCam is impossible and unnecessary — /// probe only which lenses have a multicam format, then use the chosen one as the /// single back input. private func discoverBackLenses () { var found : [ BackLens ] = [] for lens in BackLens . allCases { guard let device = Self . device ( for : lens ) else { continue } guard device . formats . contains ( where : { $0 . isMultiCamSupported }) else { continue } found . append ( lens ) } availableBackLenses = found if ! found . contains ( backLens ) { backLens = found . contains ( . wide ) ? . wide : ( found . first ?? . wide ) } } Front camera zoom, incidentally, is 1.0 and stays 1.0: there is no optical zoom there, so videoMaxZoomFactor is 1. If the front camera is your main frame, pinch-to-zoom does nothing, and the honest move is to say so rather than let a gesture look broken. What actually works One clock, one texture Two camera streams do not arrive in lockstep. The design that avoids an entire class of bugs is to treat one camera as the clock and hold only the latest frame from the other, then render one texture that is used for both the preview and the writer: func captureOutput ( _ output : AVCaptureOutput , didOutput sampleBuffer : CMSampleBuffer , from connection : AVCaptureConnection ) { if output is AVCaptureAudioDataOutput { if recorder . isRecording { recorder . appendAudio ( sampleBuffer ) } return } guard let pixelBuffer = CMSampleBufferGetImageBuffer ( sampleBuffer ) else { return } guard isBack ( output ) else { latestFront = pixelBuffer // front camera: keep only the newest frame return } // the back camera is the clock guard let front = latestFront else { return } let pool : CVPixelBufferPool ? = recorder . isRecording ? recorder . pixelBufferPool : nil if let composed = compositor . render ( back : pixelBuffer , front : front , recordingPool : pool ) { recorder . appendVideo ( composed , pts : CMSampleBufferGetPresentationTimeStamp ( sampleBuffer )) } } The composite is rendered directly into a buffer taken from the asset writer's pixelBufferPool , and that texture is then sampled to the screen. Preview and recording are structurally incapable of disagreeing. Splitting this into two independent render paths as an "optimisation" reintroduces the worst bug class in this domain: looks right on screen, wrong in the file. All three outputs share one serial data queue and never touch the main actor. Treat resilience as four named failure paths Four things end a dual recording, and each one destroys the file if unhandled: path consequence if ignored session interrupted (call, another app takes the camera) AVAssetWriter stuck half-open, corrupt file mediaServicesWereReset reusing old inputs/outputs silently stops delivering frames — no error, the picture just freezes thermal state reaches .critical the system kills the session; the whole in-progress take is lost storage fills writer fails outright, entire recording lost The mediaServicesWereReset one is the nastiest because there is no error at all — you must rebuild the whole session. And all automatic stops must funnel through the same finalize path the user's own stop button uses. A second teardown path is how you get one code path that saves the file and another that doesn't. The thermal and storage policies are pure functions, which is the only way they get tested: enum CapturePolicy { static let videoBitrate : Int = 10_000_000 static let minBytesToStart : Int64 = 200 * 1024 * 1024 static let minBytesToContinue : Int64 = 100 * 1024 * 1024 static func thermalAction ( level : ThermalLevel , isRecording : Bool , isHD1080 : Bool ) -> ThermalAction { switch level { case . critical : return isRecording ? . stopRecording : . none case . serious : if ! isRecording , isHD1080 { return . dropTo720 } return . none case . nominal , . fair : return . none } } } The asymmetry is deliberate: at serious , drop to 720p only if you have not started yet — starting a heavy take on an already-hot phone is how you get an interrupted one — but if you are already recording, warn rather than yank the resolution mid-file. Focus coordinates, the silent inversion focusPointOfInterest is expressed in the unrotated landscape sensor frame . It does not follow videoRotationAngle or isVideoMirrored . Converting from a normalised portrait canvas point: back camera (rotation 90): (u, v) = (y, 1 - x) front camera (rotation 90 + mirrored): (u, v) = (y, x) Get it backwards and nothing crashes and nothing logs. Tapping the top-left just focuses the bottom-right. This is why that conversion is a pure function with dozens of tests — and those tests were mutation-verified: swapping the front/back formulas makes them fail immediately. There is still a hole worth being honest about. The tests lock the contract of the pure function, and the contract assumes both connections set videoRotationAngle = 90 with the front additionally mirrored. Change those two lines in the session and every test stays green while focus is inverted on a real phone. Costs and boundaries Nothing camera-related can be verified in the simulator. AVCaptureMultiCamSession.isMultiCamSupported is permanently false there, so
the app correctly shows an unsupported-device screen. Every capture change needs
a real A12-or-later device. (Do not hardcode a model list — that system flag is
the only authority. Apple documents A12+, which is where "iPhone XS/XR or newer"
comes from, but the flag is what you branch on.) Heat and battery are materially worse than single-camera recording. Two
sensors, two ISP paths, a Metal composite per frame and an encoder. Users notice. Layout crops. Side-by-side portrait means fitting a 720×1280 source into a
540×1920 column — 25% is lost from each side. That is arithmetic, not a bug, but
it must be designed around. Some things get frozen at record time. Muting is implemented by not creating
an audio track at start() , which is more robust than writing a silent track, so
it cannot be toggled mid-recording. Aspect ratio likewise cannot change during a
take without destroying the writer. Metal has its own traps here. half is a builtin type name and cannot be a
variable (the compiler error is wildly misleading); multiple draw calls must use setVertexBytes / setFragmentBytes rather than sharing one MTLBuffer at
offset 0; and CVMetalTexture objects must be kept alive until the command
buffer completes. iOS 17+ blocks the easy device screenshot path , so visual verification of a
camera app is manual. Plan for it. This is the capture stack behind DualCam, an iOS app that records both cameras into a single composited file.
items.summary_html:
Modern iPhones can genuinely run the front and back cameras at the same time.
AVCaptureMultiCamSession has been in the SDK since iOS 13 and works on A12 and
later hardware. And yet Apple's own Camera app has no dual-recording mode, no
toggle, no hidden gesture.

That is not a product oversight you can route around. iOS has two separate
concepts: a normal AVCaptureSession runs exactly one camera and can switch
between them, and a multi-camera session runs several inputs concurrently. The
second is a different object with different rules, and almost everything you know
about the first one is wrong for it.

Here is what those rules actually cost, from a shipping dual-camera recorder.

The problem

You want one MP4 containing both cameras, composited live, with a preview that
matches the file. The pieces sound routine: two inputs, two outputs, a compositor,
an AVAssetWriter.

Why the obvious approach fails addInput / addOutput simply fail

The convenience API implicitly forms connections for you. On a multi-cam session
that fails outright. You must add inputs and outputs without connections and wire
AVCaptureConnection objects yourself:

private func addVideoBranch(device: AVCaptureDevice,
                            output: AVCaptureVideoDataOutput,
                            mirrored: Bool) throws {
    let input = try AVCaptureDeviceInput(device: device)
    guard session.canAddInput(input) else { throw ConfigError.cannotAdd("\(device.position) input") }
    session.addInputWithNoConnections(input)

    output.videoSettings = [kCVPixelBufferPixelFormatTypeKey as String: kCVPixelFormatType_32BGRA]
    output.alwaysDiscardsLateVideoFrames = true
    guard session.canAddOutput(output) else { throw ConfigError.cannotAdd("\(device.position) output") }
    session.addOutputWithNoConnections(output)

    guard let port = input.ports(for: .video,
                                 sourceDeviceType: device.deviceType,
                                 sourceDevicePosition: device.position).first else {
        throw ConfigError.noPort("\(device.position)")
    }

    let conn = AVCaptureConnection(inputPorts: [port], output: output)
    guard session.canAddConnection(conn) else { throw ConfigError.cannotAdd("\(device.position) connection") }
    session.addConnection(conn)

    if conn.isVideoRotationAngleSupported(90) { conn.videoRotationAngle = 90 }
    if mirrored, conn.isVideoMirroringSupported {
        conn.automaticallyAdjustsVideoMirroring = false
        conn.isVideoMirrored = true
    }
}
sessionPreset does not work either

A multi-cam session only accepts .inputPriority. Resolution is chosen per device
by picking an activeFormat, only from formats where isMultiCamSupported == true
— and it must be chosen before addInput:

private func configureFormat(for device: AVCaptureDevice, targetWidth: Int32) throws {
    let multiCamFormats = device.formats.filter { $0.isMultiCamSupported }
    guard !multiCamFormats.isEmpty else { throw ConfigError.noFormat("\(device.position)") }

    func supports30fps(_ f: AVCaptureDevice.Format) -> Bool {
        f.videoSupportedFrameRateRanges.contains { $0.minFrameRate <= 30 && $0.maxFrameRate >= 30 }
    }
    func dims(_ f: AVCaptureDevice.Format) -> CMVideoDimensions {
        CMVideoFormatDescriptionGetDimensions(f.formatDescription)
    }

    let chosen = multiCamFormats.first(where: { dims($0).width == targetWidth && supports30fps($0) })
        ?? multiCamFormats.max(by: { a, b in
            Int(dims(a).width) * Int(dims(a).height) < Int(dims(b).width) * Int(dims(b).height)
        })!

    try device.lockForConfiguration()
    defer { device.unlockForConfiguration() }
    device.activeFormat = chosen
    let duration = CMTime(value: 1, timescale: 30)
    device.activeVideoMinFrameDuration = duration
    device.activeVideoMaxFrameDuration = duration
}

Note filter { $0.isMultiCamSupported }. The set of multi-cam formats is a strict
subset of what the device offers when it is the only camera running. This is the
first place the "why not just do what the Camera app does" answer starts to appear:
the Camera app is not choosing from the same menu.

The hardwareCost gate — and it cannot be pre-checked

This is the constraint that shapes the whole feature. A multi-cam configuration has
a hardwareCost and a systemPressureCost. If hardwareCost > 1.0 you get a
runtime error and the session dies. And the value only reflects the new
configuration after you commit it. There is no dry run.

So every configuration change has to be: change → commit → read cost → roll back if
over.

session.beginConfiguration()
do {
    try configureFormat(for: back,  targetWidth: r.targetWidth)
    try configureFormat(for: front, targetWidth: r.targetWidth)
} catch {
    session.commitConfiguration()
    errorMessage = L10n.Error.detail(Strings.resolutionFailed, error.localizedDescription)
    await startSession()
    return
}
session.commitConfiguration()

if session.hardwareCost > 1.0 {
    downgraded = true
    applied = previous
    session.beginConfiguration()
    try? configureFormat(for: back,  targetWidth: previous.targetWidth)
    try? configureFormat(for: front, targetWidth: previous.targetWidth)
    session.commitConfiguration()
}

Dual 1080p exceeds the budget easily on many devices. That rollback is not
defensive tidiness — remove it and you ship an app that dies when a user picks a
resolution their phone cannot sustain.

The seamless zoom is not available to you

The stock Camera app's continuous pinch from ultra-wide through wide to telephoto
is built on a virtual capture device that internally owns several physical lenses
and crossfades between them. A multi-cam session connects to specific physical
devices, because that is what the isMultiCamSupported format check operates on. A
virtual device that silently reaches across several lenses is not something that
check can reason about.

The consequence for the UI is that lens choice and zoom become two different
controls, and the lens picker may list fewer lenses than the stock app shows:

/// Running three back lenses at once under MultiCam is impossible and unnecessary —
/// probe only which lenses have a multicam format, then use the chosen one as the
/// single back input.
private func discoverBackLenses() {
    var found: [BackLens] = []
    for lens in BackLens.allCases {
        guard let device = Self.device(for: lens) else { continue }
        guard device.formats.contains(where: { $0.isMultiCamSupported }) else { continue }
        found.append(lens)
    }
    availableBackLenses = found
    if !found.contains(backLens) {
        backLens = found.contains(.wide) ? .wide : (found.first ?? .wide)
    }
}

Front camera zoom, incidentally, is 1.0 and stays 1.0: there is no optical zoom
there, so videoMaxZoomFactor is 1. If the front camera is your main frame,
pinch-to-zoom does nothing, and the honest move is to say so rather than let a
gesture look broken.

What actually works One clock, one texture

Two camera streams do not arrive in lockstep. The design that avoids an entire
class of bugs is to treat one camera as the clock and hold only the latest frame
from the other, then render one texture that is used for both the preview and
the writer:

func captureOutput(_ output: AVCaptureOutput,
                   didOutput sampleBuffer: CMSampleBuffer,
                   from connection: AVCaptureConnection) {

    if output is AVCaptureAudioDataOutput {
        if recorder.isRecording { recorder.appendAudio(sampleBuffer) }
        return
    }

    guard let pixelBuffer = CMSampleBufferGetImageBuffer(sampleBuffer) else { return }

    guard isBack(output) else {
        latestFront = pixelBuffer   // front camera: keep only the newest frame
        return
    }

    // the back camera is the clock
    guard let front = latestFront else { return }

    let pool: CVPixelBufferPool? = recorder.isRecording ? recorder.pixelBufferPool : nil
    if let composed = compositor.render(back: pixelBuffer, front: front, recordingPool: pool) {
        recorder.appendVideo(composed, pts: CMSampleBufferGetPresentationTimeStamp(sampleBuffer))
    }
}

The composite is rendered directly into a buffer taken from the asset writer's
pixelBufferPool, and that texture is then sampled to the screen. Preview and
recording are structurally incapable of disagreeing. Splitting this into two
independent render paths as an "optimisation" reintroduces the worst bug class in
this domain: looks right on screen, wrong in the file.

All three outputs share one serial data queue and never touch the main actor.

Treat resilience as four named failure paths

Four things end a dual recording, and each one destroys the file if unhandled:

path consequence if ignored session interrupted (call, another app takes the camera) AVAssetWriter stuck half-open, corrupt file mediaServicesWereReset reusing old inputs/outputs silently stops delivering frames — no error, the picture just freezes thermal state reaches .critical the system kills the session; the whole in-progress take is lost storage fills writer fails outright, entire recording lost

The mediaServicesWereReset one is the nastiest because there is no error at all —
you must rebuild the whole session. And all automatic stops must funnel through the
same finalize path the user's own stop button uses. A second teardown path is how
you get one code path that saves the file and another that doesn't.

The thermal and storage policies are pure functions, which is the only way they get
tested:

enum CapturePolicy {
    static let videoBitrate: Int = 10_000_000
    static let minBytesToStart: Int64 = 200 * 1024 * 1024
    static let minBytesToContinue: Int64 = 100 * 1024 * 1024

    static func thermalAction(level: ThermalLevel, isRecording: Bool, isHD1080: Bool) -> ThermalAction {
        switch level {
        case .critical:
            return isRecording ? .stopRecording : .none
        case .serious:
            if !isRecording, isHD1080 { return .dropTo720 }
            return .none
        case .nominal, .fair:
            return .none
        }
    }
}

The asymmetry is deliberate: at serious, drop to 720p only if you have not
started yet — starting a heavy take on an already-hot phone is how you get an
interrupted one — but if you are already recording, warn rather than yank the
resolution mid-file.

Focus coordinates, the silent inversion

focusPointOfInterest is expressed in the unrotated landscape sensor frame. It
does not follow videoRotationAngle or isVideoMirrored. Converting from a
normalised portrait canvas point:

  • back camera (rotation 90): (u, v) = (y, 1 - x)
  • front camera (rotation 90 + mirrored): (u, v) = (y, x)

Get it backwards and nothing crashes and nothing logs. Tapping the top-left just
focuses the bottom-right. This is why that conversion is a pure function with
dozens of tests — and those tests were mutation-verified: swapping the front/back
formulas makes them fail immediately.

There is still a hole worth being honest about. The tests lock the contract of the
pure function, and the contract assumes both connections set
videoRotationAngle = 90 with the front additionally mirrored. Change those two
lines in the session and every test stays green while focus is inverted on a real
phone.

Costs and boundaries
  • Nothing camera-related can be verified in the simulator. AVCaptureMultiCamSession.isMultiCamSupported is permanently false there, so the app correctly shows an unsupported-device screen. Every capture change needs a real A12-or-later device. (Do not hardcode a model list — that system flag is the only authority. Apple documents A12+, which is where "iPhone XS/XR or newer" comes from, but the flag is what you branch on.)
  • Heat and battery are materially worse than single-camera recording. Two sensors, two ISP paths, a Metal composite per frame and an encoder. Users notice.
  • Layout crops. Side-by-side portrait means fitting a 720×1280 source into a 540×1920 column — 25% is lost from each side. That is arithmetic, not a bug, but it must be designed around.
  • Some things get frozen at record time. Muting is implemented by not creating an audio track at start(), which is more robust than writing a silent track, so it cannot be toggled mid-recording. Aspect ratio likewise cannot change during a take without destroying the writer.
  • Metal has its own traps here. half is a builtin type name and cannot be a variable (the compiler error is wildly misleading); multiple draw calls must use setVertexBytes/setFragmentBytes rather than sharing one MTLBuffer at offset 0; and CVMetalTexture objects must be kept alive until the command buffer completes.
  • iOS 17+ blocks the easy device screenshot path, so visual verification of a camera app is manual. Plan for it.

This is the capture stack behind DualCam, an iOS app that records both cameras into
a single composited file.

items.title: The three hard constraints of an iOS keyboard extension
items.summary:
A custom keyboard on iOS looks like a small UIKit app. It is not. It is a UIInputViewController living inside an extension process with rules that no normal app has to obey, and the three that actually shape the code are: a memory ceiling in the tens of megabytes, enforced by silent termination; a sandbox that is off by default ( Allow Full Access ), which removes
networking, location, the system pasteboard — and, less obviously, a reliably writable App Group container; a feedback path (sound + haptics) that must be produced without an audio
session, inside the same tight budget, on the keystroke path. Everything below is from a shipping keyboard extension. The numbers are device measurements, not estimates, and several of them are numbers that proved an earlier hypothesis wrong. Constraint 1: the memory ceiling, and why you cannot debug it normally The ceiling for a keyboard extension is somewhere around 60MB of phys_footprint . What makes it hard is not the size — it is the failure mode. When you cross it, jetsam kills the extension: no crash log, no signal, no exception. iOS just switches the user back to the previously used keyboard. From the user's side, "the keyboard quit by itself, mid-sentence". From your side, there is nothing to read afterwards. An empty subclass with an empty view survives every cycle in a leak harness while a plain UIViewController survives none. A device probe reported exactly one live controller, which seemed to exonerate the controller — but both facts are true at once: iOS builds a new controller for each host app the keyboard appears in , releases the old one (hence the count of one), and keeps every one of their views. Checkpoints inside viewDidLoad , which only run for a fresh controller, read 70MB . A brand-new keyboard was being built on top of everything its predecessors left behind, and no cache purge touches it, because a retained view is not a cache. Fifty key buttons with a gradient, a glow layer and a rasterised shadow each is about 3MB — exactly the per-cycle delta the device reported. The fix is to empty the view in deinit , deferred one main-queue turn rather than done inside dealloc . Doing the same teardown in viewWillDisappear is wrong: the same controller is hidden and re-shown many times, so that version pays a rebuild every time and feeds UIKit's own unpurgeable caches. With it off, an extension has no network, no location, and no system pasteboard. The keyboard's copy/paste buttons therefore cannot silently do nothing: /// The system pasteboard is only reachable with Full Access. If it's off we /// say so rather than doing nothing. private func requireFullAccessForClipboard () -> Bool { if hasFullAccess { return true } showToast ( "Turn on Full Access for copy & paste" ) return false } The non-obvious cost is storage.
